title: Fallout: Wasteland Warfare second edition captures the best part of the Bethesda games
content:
If Fallout: Wasteland Warfare 2nd edition has successfully adapted just one thing right from the Bethesda videogames, it's the sense of discovery. I'm early in my playtesting for this solo and co-op first adventure wargame, but its idiosyncratic gameplay reminds me of my very favorite parts of Fallouts 3 and 4 - heading out into the wasteland with absolutely no idea what I'm going to find.

With the starter set for Fallout: Wasteland Warfare second edition expected to launch in February 2027, I'm playing with PDF rulebooks, minis from the substantial range from the game's first edition and the sibling game Fallout Factions, and a custom dice app: thanks to Modiphius for providing the rules PDFs and a lot of the minis. I'm pretty green when it comes to solo wargames and game modes, so my apologies to genre veterans if everything I point out is bleeding obvious.

Wasteland Warfare 2nd edition is admin heavy, and I mean that as a complement. As well as picking a hero and recruiting their followers, your campaign starts by defining your wasteland. It's a lot like doing DM prep for D&D: you're going to create a list of possible factions that your wanderers could run into, and populate the spawn tables for the AI-controlled enemies you'll face if you ever comes to blows, choices you'll tailor to your available model collection.

These random result tables are then used when you set out to explore the wasteland. You'll keep track of your journey by filling in a map divided into squares (much like the maps in Fallout 1 and 2). The point of interest in each location is generated when you come to it, and you'll roll to see which faction is currently squatting there, and the mission you'll play against them if they're hostile.

Side quests, story quests, and faction quests are available from settlements, which inject additional mission objectives in specific locations, even spawning those locations into your map if they don't already exist. Travel far enough and you'll cross into new regions, facing tougher enemies and new conditions.

In my test games with my buddy Justin our survivor hero and their hunter friend began their journey tyring to find and repair vital infrastructure for their settlement. They first clashed with raiders in a deserted settlement to the north, before striking east and making it to a radio tower.

There, the weirdly patriotic DJ told them of a settlement a few clicks to the east, promising a good meal. En route they were ambushed at a crossroads gas station by the much-diminished local chapter of the Brotherhood of Steel. Vanquishing their novitiates and claiming a cache of good quality armor, the duo at last made it to the gates of the promised settlement, only to see ominous signs that it was now a lair of super mutants…

The game has a lopsided rhythm: exploration is a muttered affair of rolling dice, referencing books, keeping records, and talking to a friend (or yourself) to rationalise events into an emerging story; fights are comparatively lengthy and involved, though small by wargaming standards. Justin and I ran through a series of battles in one sitting with the models and terrain I had on hand.

Now that I've switched to solo play, I'm considering the hobby preparations for each new encounter - like making custom terrain and painting new minis - just as much a part of the experience of the game. The point is wallowing in the Fallout atmosphere, whether preparing for a fight or in it.

That resonates a lot with my experiences with the Bethesda Fallouts. Fallout 3 was the game I bought an XBox 360 for, and I rinsed the map without ever finishing the main story. I was there for the vibes, the environmental storytelling, the strange encounters waiting around every corner. By the time Fallout 4 rolled around I had grown pretty jaded with Bethesda's storytelling and quest design, but I still can't fault its worldbuilding chops.

If Wasteland Warfare second edition only succeeds in capturing that part of the Fallout experience, it will still have captured my favorite part of the games.

Did you play Wasteland Warfare first edition? Do you have another favorite solo or co-op wargame? Share your thoughts in the Wargamer Discord community!

title: Deployed and Ready - Deployment Basics in StarCraft: The Miniatures Game
content:
As StarCraft gains momentum in the ever growing miniatures game community, we have to start considering, “what makes this game unique?” Theme is a great way to pull people in but mechanics are often what keep our interest. Let’s take a minute to discuss a deceptively complex aspect of StarCraft: Deployment.

Why Is Deployment Important?

The main reasons are tempo and control. To win StarCraft, you have to score points by either eliminating your opponents models or by controlling scenario zones and objectives. As with most wargames, positioning is important. What quadrant of the board you are in often matters, objective markers have a set distance that you need to be within, and deployment varies game to game.

The question remains, how do we use deployment to set the tempo of the game and control the battlefield?

Let's start with the basics. StarCraft begins with selecting not only a scenario but a specific deployment card. Here are a couple of examples:

Credit: Archon Studios
Credit: Archon Studios

Both players bring two options and one player bans two of the four options. The other player will then select between the remaining two options. The deployment zones are anything but standard. Sometimes you are on the far end of the map giving an advantage to ranged models such as Terran Marine spam. Occasionally you are deploying in opposite corners giving slow moving roaches an easy time setting up on points and engaging the enemy. Don’t ignore the importance of deployment! Make sure you bring zones that benefit what your army is trying to accomplish.

How Does Deployment Work?

The StarCraft miniatures game comes from a PC real-time strategy game, and one of the skills that game required you to learn was how to build your base and your army. The miniatures game's rules help list building and deployment accurately represent that initial strategy. When deploying, you must select a board edge that is within your zone, either red or blue. Something that often catches players off guard is that your models don’t start on the map. This means that anything that can impact your models, such as a buff to speed with creep, doesn’t apply until after the models have been deployed. Deployment must be from a board edge you control and the model will walk on using their current speed.

Despite a nearby creep token, these Roaches still only move 4" onto the board.

What’s fascinating is that the term “board edge” can often be applied to things not just in your zone. Take the Protoss Pylon for example. Once this model has been on the battlefield for a full round, it can then deploy models from it as if it was a board edge.

Models deployed from a Pylon treat it's base as a board edge

This can really open up your angle of attack as you suddenly have models further up the field and able to engage earlier. There are rules to keep in mind about these unique deployment strategies. The most common rule is that the temporary board edge often can’t be placed within 10” of an enemy model. And did you also wonder why those L brackets were used? Well, they mark each player's starting zone, and enemy units can't end any deployment there.

The Zerg token must be placed further then 10 from an enemy and not in the Protoss deployment zone

Tempo

The concept of "tempo" has existed since before gaming existed, but that's because it was a musical term first: It's the speed and pace of the beat in a piece of music. It applies to StarCraft by setting the speed of the game, often done with your choice of scenario. Still, deployment will set a tempo as well as you must first decide what models you want to deploy.

Yes, that statement might feel like it’s self-evident, but it's still important to consider what you deploy and how it affects your tempo. This is especially relevant as passing for priority is a major part of StarCraft gameplay and strategy. Protoss vs Terran is a great example on how tempo can impact a game. With Terran, you can likely put out 4 or 5 units on the first turn while Protoss might only put out 3. The tempo is already shifted with Terran having more options of activations while Protoss will often gain the advantage of getting to activate first. If Terran want to compete with Protoss on taking the first activation, they will often have to do it by sacrificing activations of other models. For making attacks, this is crucial!

When you deploy, you have to consider what the goal of the game is and if putting out your 2 supply Zealot is a good idea when you can only place 5 supply. Is there only one real objective to fight over? Fewer models might work then as you don’t need to spread yourself thin. Are you having to control multiple quadrants plus markers? Then you should consider deploying lower supply count models to have more influence on the board. Supply is everything in this game!

Control

Tempo directly leads to your control on the board. Let's continue our theory crafting of Terran vs your Protoss models on Gauntlet.

The Gauntlet deployment card | Credit: Archon Studios

The deployment on this map is extremely wide and depending on how much starting supply you get, it might be difficult to control all of the board vs Terran. They might have 2 full units in both upper quadrants. But because this is an alternating activation game, deployment doesn’t have to happen all at once and you can be flexible in your decisions. The Pylon and Warp Prism are fantastic options to apply pressure in spots your opponents leave vulnerable. An interesting first turn strategy is to use the Warp Prism tactical card to place a faction token on one of your opponent's objective markers to threaten placing something sturdy contesting enemy lines. Sure, the models don’t come down until after scoring, but it means they can avoid the long march up, and many scenarios don't even score in the first round. You just need to be careful not to place within 10” of an enemy model.

By applying pressure to your opponent's markers and quadrants, you force them to react in ways that might place their units in poor positions. You are not required to place anything with the Warp Prism, after all! It’s these back and forth reactions that make StarCraft an interesting wargame. StarCraft rewards players for out-of-the-box thinking and exploiting their opponents' poor positioning, arguably making Deployment the most important concept to understand first.

We haven’t even touched on how models can be removed from the table to be redeployed later! While a common tactic in Protoss, it’s an option available to the other factions as well. It’s a frustrating moment when you have all but one model dead in a unit of Raynor’s Raiders and then your opponent just medevacs him away with the Dropship tactical card's Ready for Dust-off ability. Come back here with my supply point!

That being said, don’t think you can just hide your injured supply off the table. Anything not deployed at the end of the game will score points for your opponent so be sure to at least have them out there somewhere!

Final Thoughts

Deployment in StarCraft will form a crucial part of your strategy, and we've only touched on the basics here. If you want to find success, you'll need to have a solid grasp not only on what units to bring in and where to deploy them, but when to deploy them to make sure you're able to get the most value out of them. Making use of all of the tools available to you to set the tempo early and keep control of key segments of the board will be crucial if you want to establish dominance over the Koprulu sector.

Have any questions or feedback? Drop us a note in the comments below or email us at contact@tabletopbattles.com. Want articles like this linked in your inbox every Monday morning? Sign up for our newsletter. title: Detachment Focus: Warpstrike Champions (Updated November 3, 2026)
content:
In this series of articles we take a deep dive into a specific Detachment for a faction, covering the faction’s rules and upgrades and talking about how to build around that faction for competitive play. In this article, we’re covering the Warpstrike Champions Detachment for Chaos Space Marines.

Do you want a Detachment that pushes you to play Chaos Terminators? Have you been itching for something that really makes Obliterators and the Mutilators pop? Do you want something that's vaguely Iron Warriors-coded but better than Fellhammer Siege Host? Well then good news - Warpstrike Champions might be the Detachment for you.

Changelog

  • 11-3-2026: Updated for 11th edition
  • 4-1-2026: Initial Publication

Detachment Cost: 2 DP

Disposition: Disruption

The Warpstrike Champions Detachment is all about buffing your Terminators, Obliterators, and Mutilators, really pairing with Kravek Morne - albeit in a more indirect fashion than some of the other faction-themed Detachments. This one lets you pull your bulky infantry up off the table to deep strike again later, and has a number of effects for when they arrive on the table, plus some effects just for buffing Terminators, Mutilators, and Obliterators. The net effect is that some of the faction's best units - namely Terminators and Mutilators - get their best effects here - while the 2 DP cost means you can still pair it with Cabal of Chaos, further buffing them in important ways.

Detachment Rule: Warp Portals

At the end of your opponent's turn, you pick a number of TERMINATOR, OBLITERATOR, and MUTILATOR units from your army (except for units within Engagement Range of an enemy unit) - those units go back into Strategic Reserves. You can pick one unit in Incursion games, two in Strike Force, and three in Onslaught.

This is a very powerful ability, and one you just don't see much in Chaos Space Marines outside of Warp Talons. Terminators, Mutilators, and Obliterators just don't have good movement (Obliterators only go 4"), and being able to pick up and reposition is a really powerful ability when you're focusing on ranged damage output - something that Cabal of Chaos will naturally push you to do. There are plenty of times where your opponent may leave you an interesting target in a far-off corner but actually dropping in over there with deep strike and killing it will mean being too far away from other targets and struggling to make more of an impact. Now you can simply pick them up and drop them back in again.

The standard move with this ability is to have a key unit on the table turn 1 and then pick them up in your opponent's first turn. If they went first, you'll be able to drop your unit in for a turn 1 deep strike on your turn, potentially getting the jump on them in a key spot. With the right mix of units on the table, you'll never be out of position to reach key objectives, and it's worth pointing out that you can use this just fine with a single model Terminator Lord or Sorcerer, picking them up and dropping them down in key places to do actions or score secondary objectives. Terminator Chaos Lords are particularly great at this since they halve incoming damage.

The September balance update really changed the math on this Detachment, by making Terminator shooting very good. Combi-bolters suddenly being S5 AP-1 means that they can be buffed to AP-2 with help from the Death Hex on a Sorcerer in Terminator Armour, and that gives them Scarab-like levels of damage output with Dark Pacts and full re-rolls to hit, but at a cut-rate price.

Something to note is that it's possible to use Abaddon to pick up a unit of Chosen with this rule, but they'll have to re-enter from the battlefield edge when doing so. You can also use it to pick up Huron's unit if he's attached to a unit of Terminators but note that you can't attach the Masters of the Maelstrom to his unit if you're doing that. In a similar fashion, there are several effects here which are good on Raptors, Warp Talons, or a Winged Daemon Prince.

Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Enhancements

All four of these Enhancements are meant to interact with Deep Strike units, making them ideal for Terminator Chaos Lords and Sorcerers, but it's worth noting that Jump Pack Lords can make use of these as well. There's no way to get these effects on a unit of Obliterators or Mutilators. These are also ironically great on Jump Pack Chaos Lords, who can lead Deep Strike units of their own.

  • Infernal Fulgurite (20 points) – Non-DAMNED model only. Once per battle, the bearer's unit can be targeted with Rapid Ingress for 0 CP, and you can target them with it even if you've already targeted another unit; 

This is really solid, though more limited than you'd expect - there's no way to get it onto units of Mutilators or Obliterators (Morne is an EPIC HERO) - so if you want to use it with the Detachment rule it'll mean putting it on a Terminator Lord or Terminator Sorcerer, and that's probably where you most want it, since it will let you drop in alongside another unit and make the most of the rule.

That said if you want to be different you can throw this on a Jump Pack Chaos Lord and use it to Rapid Ingress a unit of Raptors. This isn't a good move and I wouldn't recommend it, but it's certainly entertaining and unexpected.

  • Eye of the Warp (15 points) – Deep Strike model only. Every time the bearer's unit is set up on the battlefield, you can re-roll Charge rolls for that unit until the end of the turn.

This one's a bit of a mixed bag. On the one hand, if you're going to try and charge out of Deep Strike, you need this - adding a re-roll to the mix takes your odds from 23% to 49%, and combining it with Portal of Spite for +2 to your Charge roll makes your odds close to 83% with a re-roll, and that's great. This is another one that's great on a unit of Raptors with a Jump Pack Lord but note that it's also active any time you're set up on the table. This means that if you put it on a Lord in a Land Raider, it'll apply when they Disembark, giving you re-rolls to the charge. That's pretty nifty. But you already get this ability from Terminator Sorcerers, and you're going to take those if you're running Cabal of Chaos.

  • Akshur's Binding Runes (20 points) – Deep Strike model only. The bearer's unit can be set up with Deep Strike in the Movement phase of your first, second, or third turns, regardless of any mission rules. 

Now we're talking. Turn 1 Deep Strikes can be really powerful, letting you deploy a unit wherever it'll do the most damage, and if you combine this with something like Portal of Spite you can get off some nasty turn 1 charges.

  • Tzagulla (25 points) – Deep Strike model only. The bearer gets +1 Attacks, Strength, and AP on all of its weapons. Additionally, each time you set up the bearer's unit on the Battlefield from Reserves, they get +1 Damage as well. 

This is a very powerful upgrade, in part because it affects all of the bearer's weapons and not just their melee weapons. This is really good on a Terminator Sorcerer, who has a realy solid shooting attack with Infernal Gaze (and suddenly being S7 AP-3 or -4, D3+1 damage is really nasty, plus his 2-damage combi-weapon, all with full re-rolls to hit).

The other place you want to put this? On a Winged Daemon Prince. These are great buffs to drop on the model, and if you're going this route, you'll either to dedicate him to Khorne (+2 Strength), or Tzeentch (+3A on his Infernal Cannon). The former gives you a nasty melee threat, able to drop out seven attacks at S11, AP-3, and 4 damage on the turns you arrive from deep strike. Those will rely on making deep strike charges and so if you want something more reliable going with Tzeentch means his cannon will throw out 6 shots at S6 AP-2, 3 damage - a nasty melee attack to work with.

On the whole you probably get more value out of this on a Terminator Sorcerer since he has the ability to go back up with his unit over and over and extra damage on the shooting attack is going to do more for you than extra damage on the melee weapons.

Also I refuse to say the name of this Enhancement any way other than as rhyming with "Dragula" so I can mentally sing the song whenever my unit drops in and burns through some witches.

Obliterators. Credit: Rockfish

Stratagems

This is a suite of stratagems built for your Deep Strike units. Three only work on Terminator/Obliterator/Mutilator units and they're generally geared toward a mix of movement tricks and defensive buffs.

  • Empyric Dislocation (Battle Tactic, 1 CP) – Used on one of your non-DAMNED units in your opponent's Shooting phase or the Fight phase after an enemy picks its targets. Until the end of the activation, incoming attacks reduce their AP by 1. You can't use this on a unit on which you used Armour of Corruption. 

This renamed Armour of Contempt is a fine ability, and great for protecting a unit. At 1 CP it's more accessible than Armour of Corruption, and the timing is much more generous. Given you'll be running a lot of models with a 2+ save, this is great for blanking AP-2 shooting attacks when you have cover. This notably can be used on more units than Armour of Corruption, and will be good when you need to protect two units.

  • Armour of Corruption (Strategic Ploy, 2 CP) – Used in the Fight phase on a unit of Terminators, Obliterators, or Mutilators picked as a target of attacks. Until the end of the turn, incoming attacks are -1 damage against that unit. You can't double up with this and Empyric Dislocation.

This is a very powerful ability, though it's a bit costly at 2 CP given it's restricted to the Fight phase. That said, it's a really great way to just force units with 2- and 3-damage melee attacks to bounce off you, effectively killing their output. This one's useful enough that if you're running a 10-man brick of Terminators you probably either want a Chaos Lord attached to them so you can reduce its cost or a way to generate some extra Command Points (Abaddon comes to mind) so you can have this in your back pocket. Throwing this out against a charging unit of Thunderwolf Cavalry can be a huge difference maker.

  • Warp Flicker (Strategic Ploy, 1 CP) – Used in your Movement phase on a Terminator, Obliterator, or Mutilator unit. That unit can Advance and still Shoot and Charge. 

Hey it's the obligatory advance and charge Stratagem. Every army that wants to do serious melee needs this, especially one relying on units with 5" movement. What this really lets you do is Ingress, then Advance and Charge for an even shorter distance you're more likely to roll. It's also fantastic on Obliterators, where their 4" movement can make it difficult for them to close distances with key targets without Advancing, and they still want to be able to shoot and charge afterward.

  • Warp-Tainted (Strategic Ploy, 1 CP) - Used in your Movement phase on a unit of Terminators, Obliterators, or Mutilators which are in range of an objective marker you control. That objective marker stays under your control until an opponent controls it at the end of any phase.

Another very powerful ability, though gated to your big bulky units. Where this really shines is that you can use it in conjunction with the Detachment ability to drop a unit of something (probably Obliterators) on a far-off objective, sticky it on arrival, shoot, then pick up at the end of your opponent's turn to go somewhere else, forcing them to walk over there if they want to take it back. Or if you dropped a melee unit on there, walk off as you see fit. It's a great way to punish your opponent for leaving their home objective unprotected.

  • Siegebreaker Strike (Strategic Ploy, 1 CP) – Used in your Shooting phase on up to two of your units which arrived from Deep Strike this turn and haven't shot yet. Those units' ranged weapons get [IGNORES COVER] for the rest of the phase.

This is another really great buff, particularly on Obliterators, who really need Ignores Cover with their AP-2 and AP-3 firing modes. Combining it with Kravek Morne can give you AP-4 Ignores Cover shooting if you want to really wreck some 3+ save targets (and by "wreck" I mean "watch glumly as you only get 2 shots and miss with one of them"), and it's also neat on something like a Terminator unit with a Sorcerer packing the Tzagulla.

  • Portal of Spite (Battle Tactic, 1 CP) – Used in your Charge phase on a unit that arrived from Deep Strike this turn. It gets +2 to its charge rolls this phase.

This is massive, and it's part of what makes this whole Detachment worth considering. A 7" charge with a re-roll gives you an 86% success rate, and while you'll still fail some of those, it's reliable enough that you can at least plan on making one or two of those charges per game. That said, it's still going to fail one in six times, so don't over-extend yourself if you don't have to - you really, really want to use this on a unit led by a Terminator Sorcerer so you can get that sweet free re-roll.

Credit: Robert "TheChirurgeon" Jones

Playing This Detachment

You're going to run Terminators and Obliterators in this Detachment. If there's a place for Mutilators in the CSM army, it may be here but Terminators are likely to get the job done for you just fine. If you're bringing Mutilators, it's because you don't want to bring tanks and you desperately need a way to crack enemy armor - Obliterators are OK at this but just aren't great in 11th edition and so won't make your list.

This Detachment usually wants at least two big units of Terminators and it'll need characters to go with them. This used to be a tough choice, but the September balance update and Cabal of Chaos make it pretty easy - you're going to take a Sorcerer in Terminator Armour for at least one unit, and probably both. The good shooting, built-in re-rolls, and the Strength buff from the Cabal of Chaos Detachment rule just aren't matched by anything else in the army.

Let's run through your leader options real quick:

  • Abaddon. The big bad of the Chaos faction is a melee monster, and provides one of the faction's only ways to generate extra Command Points. Abaddon can also give nearby units re-rolls to hit and a 4+ invulnerable save, neither of which matters much on Terminators but he can give them re-rolls on their Leadership tests and that's pretty big for a unit which can't re-roll their pacts. Abaddon makes a good accompaniment to a smaller unit of Terminators and if you drop them in near Obliterators he can give them re-rolls on their hit rolls and make you forget that you don't have Oaths in this Detachment.
  • Kravek Morne. Morne's ability to give a unit of Terminators +1 AP is massive, and his melee output is also extremely good on its own, with the ability to re-roll wounds against a key target providing a big boost. Kravek can also join Mutilators and Obliterators, but given he lacks the shooting of the latter he's going to give you more value in terminators, where getting to AP-3 is a big deal.
  • Huron Blackheart. Huron's only got a 3+ armor save base but comes with a very good melee profile and a built-in reactive move of D3+3" that can really help Terminators pull off some nasty tricks.
  • Chaos Lord in Terminator Armour. The Chaos Lord gives his unit the ability to reduce the cost of a Stratagem by 1 once per round and halves incoming damage against his model. The real value here is the free Stratagem but what hurts this guy is that his melee output just kind of stinks. This means he's great as a cheap solo character piece who can deep strike into far-off spots and do scoring stuff, while being pretty durable against enemy shooting. I think you want one of these to act as a kind of poor man's Callidus.
  • Sorcerer in Terminator Armour. On the other hand, the Sorcerer is a much better deal, coming with two amazing abilities - the first being built-in Charge and Advance re-rolls, and the second being the Death Hex ability, which can give your entire army +1 AP against a single target for a round. That one's huge and can unlock big swings, but is also going to fail on you out of nowhere a few times per event so just be ready for it. The Sorcerer is also a great target for the Tzagulla Enhancement. On top of it, if you're running Cabal of Chaos, the Sorcerer makes your Terminators' Combi-Bolters S6 when they shoot, and that's a big deal as well.

The key here is making sure you have good support for your big, expensive units and not overdoing it. One thing to note is that Nurglings and Red Corsairs Raiders are going to be a more important piece of the puzzle with this army as you'll need them to block out Infiltrators so you can prevent them from screening out your deep strikers.

The big downside to running Cabal of Chaos + Warpstrike Champions is that you're locked into Disruption, and for that reason you don't tend to see this army outside of teams events where it can eat the Disruption spot. Veterans of the Long War is a more common play in singles events with Cabal, but ultimately feels worse in some ways as Terminators already have built-in re-rolls to hit and don't need its version of Oath of Moment.

Strengths

  • Mobility. Having the ability to go back up with two units per turn really turns a slow army into a fast one, and on top of that you have the ability to advance and charge and make charges out of deep strike.
  • Deep Strike Shenanigans. In addition to being able to charge more reliably out of Deep Strike you also have ways to drop on turn 1 and get extra Rapid Ingress, which lets you make the most of those uppy-downy abilities.
  • Defensive Buffs. Armour of Contempt and -1 damage in the fight phase are powerful effects to have which can keep your super elite infantry on the table.

Weaknesses

  • Limited Character slots. You can really only attach units to Terminators here and that means you're going to struggle getting the most out of this army's Enhancements. Further muddying the waters is that you have three great EPIC HERO units which can attach to Terminators.
  • Anti-vehicle damage. Terminators struggle to get things done against high-toughness targets. S8 is great for pulping T4 marine targets but horrible for cracking T9+ vehicles and Lethal Hits isn't the most reliable way to punch through, particularly when all you have is AP-2 2 damage attacks attached to it. 
Credit: Thomas "Goatboy" Reidy

A Sample List

We haven't seen a Warpstrike list perform well outside of Teams yet, but the list has a solid foundation and good damage output. This list comes from Nathan Roberts of team Stat Check, and was fielded at the Super 6s event in England in October. The core here is twenty Terminators, Kravek Morne and his attached Mutilators, and two Winged Daemon Princes - a ton of nasty Deep Strike threats.

Chaos Space Marines

ATTACHED UNITS

• Attached as: Leader (Character)

• Warlord

• 1x Baleflamer

• 1x Combi-bolter

• Attached as: Bodyguard

Attached unit 2

Sorcerer in Terminator Armour (110 Points)

• Attached as: Leader (Character)

• 1x Combi-bolter

• 1x Force weapon

• 1x Infernal Gaze

• Enhancements: Tzagulla

Chaos Terminator Squad (370 Points)

• Attached as: Bodyguard

• 1x Terminator Champion

• 9x Chaos Terminator

title: How to Paint Everything: Conquest Oni Kinshin
content:
The Oni Kinshin - or, as they are more commonly known, the BIG HORSES - feel like exactly what the Yoroni range needed visually. Previously, it was a two-size faction - large and huge - which somehow made the 'normal'-sized brutes feel small in comparison to the towering monsters. Each brute was the size of a mounted knight, but you didn't truly feel that looking at the army internally until you put them up alongside their version of the mounted knight.

Enter the BIG HORSES. These guys are massive - in sheer mass, they're almost like two Warhammer Rhino tanks stacked on top of each other. Despite the size, the kit is as simple as all Conquest kits are - the designers are absolutely committed to each arm and leg being a single distinct piece, with none of the complex trickery you'll see in a modern 40K kit where one piece might be a chunk of arm, leg and backpack. For that, there are minimal options or wasted plastic here - you've got four rider heads, two helmeted and two unhelmeted, four horse heads, a choice of sword or spear, and optional back banners. The massive horse body goes together in just two pieces.

There's nothing that can be done to make the double base situation elegant. Just run a line of plastic glue between them and smother the bump with texture paint - or go for something abstract as I have here.

Basing

This effect is simple and looks very unique. Step one is to get some cubes. You can find sacks of plastic cubes of varying sizes on your dropshipping site of choice for cheap; get a bunch of different sizes and glue them down in varying patterns.

My original intention with this faction was to do sharp edge highlights for a Tron-style digital reality theme, as you see in the prototype model above, but I got sick of this process practically immediately and went for something simpler and more fun.

See, the whole litany we are taught about thinning your paints? Forget that. To get this effect, grab a huge dollop of paint straight out of the pot, slap it down on the base, and then draw your brush along while spinning it a little; this'll give it a nice jagged effect at the edges. Then grab another colour and slap it down in the middle of the still-wet thick paint and drag it along as well. They'll mix (but only a bit) and settle into a cool layered effect.

The specific paints you see here are Pro Acryl Blue, Turquoise and Magenta. You can do things like slam on big thick puddles and then turn the miniature on its side to let gravity smear the paints for you. Sky's the limit!

Here's the same effect on some Warhammer models, done with a different colour selection but the same idea. While you're doing this, you're free to get wild and experimental with it - add jagged straight lines for lightning currents, huge thick pools for footprints, or even do a normal-looking texture paint/drybrush/shade around the edges to make it look like this chaotic energy is really melting out of reality. Add some snow texture, add some flowers, anything you've got spare or any paints you've accidentally got two pots of. This one's really not about the specific paints or the recipe; it's about doing everything 'wrong' because the unreality of the effect is the selling point.

One piece of advice, though - something you can do to make the colours cohere is to keep them all the same level of saturation (Saturation: How 'intense' the colour is; mixing paint with white or black will change its brightness and its saturation as the pigment is diluted; mixing a paint with its colour wheel opposite will decrease its saturation and bring it towards a neutral grey). All of the colours in the Warhammer miniatures bases are all pastels; they look like they fit together despite the hue being all over the place because they're all similarly saturated.

Painting

The BIG HORSES are drybrushing models. I don't think there's any way around that, unless you're actively insane. The huge, thick clouds of rippling hair scream out for drybrushing the fur texture into place. As a result, I found these went up shockingly fast; there are no fiddly details or painting speedbumps.

For the drybrushing, for each layer my rule of thumb is to halve the total area that you drybrushed last time - so the first layer is 50%, then 25%, then 12.5%. The exception to this is the area of key focus - almost always, the face. The horses' faces are down low, but I made sure to drybrush them up to the maximum so that they'll draw the eye.

Pink Horses

  • Pro Acryl Magenta
  • Overall wash with Magos Purple
  • Drybrush Pro Acryl Magenta
  • Drybrush Army Painter Fanatic Diviner Light - the Pro Acryl line lacks a good, strong pink; the GW Screamer Pink/Pink Horror/Emperor's Children progression works for this too.
  • Drybrush Pro Acryl Fluro Pink. This is the secret sauce; fluro paints are real sometimes foods, but adding a supernatural pop to pinks like this is exactly that use case.

Blue Horses

  • Pro Acryl Blue
  • Overall wash with Magos Purple
  • Drybrush Pro Acryl Blue
  • Drybrush Pro Acryl Turquoise
  • Drybrush Pro Acryl Blue White

The crest into white is more severe than the pink horses, so don't go nuts with it, but we need it because there aren't fluro blues.

Riders

The same process as above but I stop the drybrushing one level early; if you look at the contrast between the pink rider and the horses that's all the fluro paint.

Bronze Metals

  • Runelord Brass
  • Shade Agrax Earthshade
  • Highlight with Vallejo Imperial Gold
  • Teal details are Vallejo Beetle Green. Since the details are so small you don't actually need to do anything else with this, just let the solid colour stand.

Blacks

Your usual Black/Dark Reaper/Fenrisian Grey triad, there's no improving on perfection!

title: Warhammer 40k's biggest unofficial army app rewrote its rules: brace for chaos
content:
On Sunday, the extremely popular, free-to-use wargame army building app New Recruit announced that "due to legal reasons, official rules texts for certain games are no longer displayed on New Recruit". It hasn't specified what those legal reasons are, or listed all the games that are affected, but the original wording of all the Warhammer 40,000 rules in the app have been replaced with supermarket own-brand replacements.

New Recruit announced the changes on its website, stating the team is now "publishing our own description of how each rule works for most current games", and "older games will follow the same process". Until the process is completed, "you may see empty descriptions or [text removed]", and foreign language translations have also gone.

This is going to be an issue for the Warhammer 40k community, and possibly for other affected games. Unlike many modern wargames, accessing the full rules text for Warhammer 40,000 requires customers pay for Codex army books - a player who wants to browse the entire library of Warhammer 40k factions, whether because they want to pick a new army or they're preparing for a tournament, needs to spend over $1,000 to do so officially. Due to the new edition cycle, that investment lasts three years max. Many players choose to use New Recruit, or various other unofficial services, instead.

Warhammer 40k rules are sufficiently complex that arguments over interpretation are already common (though the modern game is blessedly well explained compared to how it has been in the past). Periodic rules changes from Games Workshop, and occasional unannounced alterations to rules text in the Warhammer app, create further misunderstandings, as the most locked-in players pick up on changes before their more casual peers. Now large portions of the player base are going to be rules text that is simply different.

It strikes me as one more good reason for Games Workshop to make more of its rules available for free. It's understandable that cost-conscious players turn to free, unofficial apps when the official one is so incomplete without spending silly money. This divides the player base, diluting the shared understanding of the rules, and creating friction.

Unofficial apps are legally permissible, at least in some forms, because of the unintuitive copyright status of game rules. The UK and US copyright regimes treats game rules in the same ways as instructions and recipes. The written text has a copyright, but the abstract process that the written text describes does not. If you've ever wondered why online recipes are so full of superfluous descriptions, this is one reason - it's to make the text less abstract and more creative, and therefore copyright protected.

Directly copying rules text into a new document is a breach of copyright, as is tweaking that text with a few changes (this is called a 'derivative work'). Yet the logical core of a set of rules has no protection. Sufficiently distinctive unofficial rules apps can therefore operate legally, assuming they don't tread on any other IP protections.

Which army building app do you use? Share your thoughts on the best, and what features - beyond price - you value, in the Wargamer Discord community.

title: Magic: The Gathering Puzzlebox – The Dilemma of Dilemmas
content:
Star Trek is on the horizon, and with it, a new named game action in the form of Facing a Dilemma. Not unlike Committing a Crime, this is a thematic batching which serves as shorthand for something most people do every game; in the case of Crimes, it's touching things which aren't yours, but for Dilemmas, it's choosing a mode(s). Unlike Crimes however, Dilemmas aren't the easiest thing to face repeatedly, and this is reflected in the card designs. For the marquee Commander of the mechanic, Seven of Nine, you could conceivably draw through your entire deck if enough problems showed up on your desk, while similar Crime payoffs require either a triggered cost or have 'once per turn' clauses. While this makes Dilemmas seem all the more exploitable, it soon becomes evident as to why the designers saw it fit to leave the action as something that didn't need limiting clauses—it's actually rather difficult to take infinite Dilemmas. Unlike Crimes, for whom cards like Hex Parasite and the like exist, you ironically lack a ton of options when building to break Dilemmas. With that in mind, let's talk about how best to use this new game action, and some...odd options, even one from Arabian Nights.

This is part of a shortform Magic series where I’m covering rapid-fire concepts about Commander that I couldn’t cover in a full Commander Focus, so if you like what you see, certainly let us know!

"...Choose one or more modes for a spell or ability."

As a refresher, Dilemmas are defined as the following: You face a dilemma as you choose one or more modes for a spell or ability. What is a mode, though? This requires we dig through the CR to find CR700.2, which defines a model piece of text as being a bulleted list following a phrase like "Choose one —". It's important to note however that unless a card has been reprinted from Khans of Tarkir or onward, it's likely that this exact phrasing is not present. Perhaps the 'choose one' is missing, or the list isn't bulleted, etc. Knowing Gatherer text is vital to actually narrowing down what cards do and don't trigger our payoffs, and does mean more cards than you'd expect fit the bill. Before we talk about some of those though, let's talk about some things which aren't Dilemmas: Council's Dilemma is an ability word and has no mechanical bearing, despite the flavor failure, and re-selecting targets or copying a card that requires you face a Dilemma does not trigger it. Dilemma triggers as a card or ability is put on the stack, when modes are chosen, and as such always resolves before the triggering effect in question. Why does that matter? Well, effects like voting or "Face a Villainous Choice —", despite having multiple potential outcomes and even the telltale em-dash, are not Dilemmas when their modes are chosen; these are selected upon the Spell's resolution, and therefore have neither the necessary bullets syntactically or timing window to count as a Dilemma. It's a bit confusing, but given the discussion I've seen online (and testing partners for some upcoming Commander Focuses) this is a common enough error that I felt it necessary to mention. As a final note for completions' sake, choosing halves for a split spell like Turn//Burn also isn't a Dilemma, which is a tragedy.

All that being said, what do help us face a ton of Dilemmas? The good news is that a Commander already exists which has used the same verbiage, from which we can draw inspiration: Riku of Many Paths. Riku has been popping up at conventions & LGSes I've attended as a fairly unique spin on spellslinger, rewarding people for playing a high density of things like Charms, Commands, and the new rebound pick-ones from Marvel Super Heroes Commander. Cards like these look quite a bit better when you staple effects like 'draw a card' onto them with Seven of Nine, or even just some drain via Elim Garak, Simple Tailor. You're confronted however with the necessity to actually cast Spells in order to face Dilemmas, however, and while it sounds a bit rich to complain about needing to cast Spells in my game of Magic, unlike Riku the revised Dilemma mechanic also calls out abilities. To that end, it turns some of these options like Seven, Elim Garak, or the 5c Captain Benjamin Sisko into more than just spellslinger Commanders, broadening their possibilities beyond that of Riku. He's still eating good from the new cards in Star Trek, mind you, but I wouldn't be covering the mechanic in such depth if all this was turned out to be a spin on Magecraft.

In a Pickle, Extra Dill-emma

Credit: Wizards of the Coast

I think when it comes to the discussion of facing Dilemmas en masse it becomes important to talk about ontological versus epistemological analysis, when it comes to Magic cards. Something I feel is especially relevant in finding the right, niche cards for a deck stems from evaluating them for what they are, rather than what they do. A great example is something like Swell of Growth in my Marwyn, the Nurturer list (which I covered here)—this is a lukewarm card, but is in fact the only Monogreen option for putting a Land into play at Instant-speed without needing something like a tap ability or to be on the field. The card itself is unimpressive, but its effect is precise and singular in what it accomplishes. When looking at cards like Relic Bind, the text of the actual Dilemma isn't what we're looking at, but instead the trigger. The ubiquity or ability to be built around behind the effect, how you actually face that Dilemma, is what matters. If you replaced the text of the card with [trigger] — face a Dilemma, does that have appeal? That's the question one needs to ask, with things like this or Crimes, where the actual effect is just gravy to the trigger (our real buildaround). With all that out of the way, it is a sick joke that I am to deliver the truth that Landfall is probably the best way to plan for Dilemmas. The most boring answer.

Feel free to print this one out.

Yes, between cards like the Retreats, Dread Presence with Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth, and even Elven Raft-Steerer from The Hobbit, the best way to see these triggers with the highest frequency is just by fetching and recurring Lands. Now, there's a bit of a silver lining here in that you're doing so in colors which normally don't play with Lands, namely Black or Dimir, and with the recent introduction of Land blinking into Blue's identity you can get a great quantity of triggers going. Copy your Retreats with things like Copy Enchantment or Mirrormade, and suddenly you're getting more value from a Land drop than Green. The alternate path is via casting spells, either noncreatures with Kykar, Zephyr Awakener, two in a turn with Cosmogrand Zenith, etc. Given you're already likely on a sufficient density of Instants & Sorceries with modes, these are slam dunk paths if you don't want to go infinite.

With that in mind, how do we go infinite with Dilemmas? There is a singular card in Magic's history which can, without need of anything other than infinite mana, cause you to face a Dilemma. No untap effects, no riders, just {2}...and controlling a Land. Let's talk, begrudgingly, about Pyramids. Printed in 1993's Arabian Nights, this is an Artifact that does something entirely unmoored from its actual text. For 2 mana, you choose one — pop an Aura on a Land, or give a Land lingering protection for the turn, removing all damage marked on it. That last one is the ticket, because you can just target the same Land, over and over, for {2}. Pyramids is however a 6-mana Artifact, and otherwise useless, so in an ideal world we're cheating its ability out via something like Trazyn the Infinite, who can himself also produce the infinite mana necessary. We can also Agatha's Soul Cauldron something like Cryptic Trilobite onto Jett Reno, Problem Solver, who receives a +1/+1 counter we can spend on 2 mana solely for abilities... receiving another when we face a Dilemma. For as bad as Pyramids is, and as pricey a real copy can be (good lord it's $120), it does represent a very specific case where it is singular in function. If you're evil, it also means you can enact one-sided MLD, but uh...don't do that.

I'm going to leave you with a few different Scryfall syntax links, which might be helpful in your quest to face Dilemmas. This looks for triggered options, and this looks for broader choices. In my search, it's quite easy to face some Dilemmas just by playing the game (Alliance-based triggers like the one on Lita, Little Orphan Amphibian are great, but cannot go infinite unless you somehow reset the trigger), but it's rather difficult to go infinite enough to end the game. That's a great show of a great mechanic, to not be so instantly-broken by Johnnies like myself. I think Dilemmas have a bright future, and while Commander options at present are functionally limited to U and/or B or 5c, I would hazard a guess we can see it return in some external product.

title: Tabletop Battles Hobby Round-Up October 2026
content:
There's a chill on the wind as October comes to a close; the autumnal air every bit as crisp as the edge highlights on our crew's models. Scroll down to see what tricks and treats await!

Rockfish

I have unfortunately had a bit of a cursed month between being busy at work and not great health things, so only a handful of things from me this time.

Trukk. Credit: Rockfish
Trukk. Credit: Rockfish
Redemptor. Credit: Rockfish
Hippogriff AFV. Credit: Rockfish
Warboss. Credit: Rockfish

Jefferson Powers

I got back to Shatterpoint this month, painting the two new boxes featuring the villains from the Ahsoka streaming series. I was especially excited about the first one, as it features Baylan Skoll and his apprentice Shin Hati, two of the most interesting Star Wars characters to come along in years.

Image credit: Jefferson Powers

The zombie Stormtroopers were probably the most fun to paint out of this batch. It's not often you get to use that much color on Imperial models.

Image credit: Jefferson Powers

"Contemptor" Kevin Stillman

The 2026 Grand Narrative is almost upon us, so I spent most of October plugging away at my Ultramarines.  The first model, of course, is a new Repulsor Executioner.  I picked this up awhile ago, so I was going to have the Space Marines' flagship tank.

Ultramarines Repulsor Executioner. Credit: Contemptor Kevin Stillman

With the new Marine Codex, the detachment I loved playing in 10th Edition, Ironstorm Spearhead, became the Iron Hands' exclusive detachment Medusa's Wrath.  However, everything I have worked on for the past year or so is in the blue and gold of Ultramar.  How was I to square this circle?  Well, several years ago I purchased Iron Father Ferrios but never got around to painting him.  Until now, when I painted him blue. I cut off the Iron Hands' specific iconography or replaced it with Ultramarines iconography, and changed his head from the pulped meat of the standard model and into the much more handsome Ultramarines upgrade sprue Terminator bare head.  And viola, we now have Master of the Forge Fennias Maxim.

The list I'm planning also requires two additional Techmarines.  While one of those will be the usual Primaris Techmarine (whom I need to build and paint or repaint an older one, to be determined), I wanted a second, different Techmarine.  While I could use the Forge World Mk. IV marine, like I did my Dark Angels, I wanted to do something different.  Then I looked in my cabinet of painted miniatures at stuff I painted during the pandemic and found the solution: the Thunderfire Cannon Techmarine.  I swiftly rebased him onto a 40, and punched up his paintjob to a modern standard:

The last full unit I painted in October was a squad of Heavy Bolter Eradicators.  These big boys were painted when I picked up my TonePro paints, and I admit I had to take the yellows out for a spin.  I used Khemri Sands 4 as a base and Hawkshroud Yellow 3 as a highlight, and the two paints blended wonderfully for purposes of making hazard stripes:

Ultramarines Eradicators with Heavy Bolters. Credit: Contemptor Kevin Stillman

November will undoubtedly consist, at least from me, of more blue Space Marines and vehicles.

SRM

Hope you aren't tired of seeing blue Space Marines in this post because by gum you're getting more.

ULtramarines Terminator Squad. Credit: SRM

Terminators are the new hotness, if you haven't heard, so it was about time I added some classic "Tactical" Terminators to my Ultramarines, replete with a 2nd edition box art-inspired scheme. These are just the crew from 10th edition's Leviathan starter set, with some light kitbashing to give Sarge a power fist and a Cyclone Missile Launcher in place of the Assault Cannon. I was kind of holding out for the Tone Pro paintline to see if I could get better coverage on my yellow for hazard stripes, but I wanted paint on them sooner.

Ultramarines Ancient in Terminator Armor. Repost. Credit: SRM

Of course, these guys need an emotional support flagbearer to make them harder to kill, and that's where the Ancient comes in. This is the fourth giant detailed banner I've painted this year, and I would like to be done painting giant detailed banners now. I'm very happy with how it came out, don't get me wrong, they're just a lot of work. The rhythms of this model were otherwise about the same as those on the Terminators before him, though I wish I'd been able to fit the sheathed Ultramarines power sword from the upgrade kit on him instead of the generic one. Guess I'll need to find some other blue guy in big armor to carry a big sword, what a challenge.

Autumn is firmly Bigg Boi Season as I'm currently taking a momentary break from the stack of six Heavy Bolter Eradicators to write this. Will they be all I can finish next month? I sure hope not!

Micah "dirtboi"

I managed to get 105 models done this month, an absolute record for myself. First up I finished 50 Shoretroopers for Star Wars legion, using mostly contrast paints and taking my time with individual rank markings. Had a ton of fun with these guys, going to field them on the table in a week for a charity event.

[gallery td_select_gallery_slide="slide" columns="2" size="full" ids="259160,259159"]

As a light little afternoon project, I speedpainted General Veers for my Blizzard Force portion of my empire army.

General Veers. Credit: dirtboi

I got quickly sidetracked from Legion models for a Saturday, having a buddy print off some models for the game Planet Shark that is absolutely adorable. He was an absolute blast to paint, and I cannot wait to paint more. I was super excited as he was an excuse to try AK Interactives plethora of water/beach basing materials, and I'm really happy with the outcome.

[gallery size="full" td_select_gallery_slide="slide" ids="259168,259169,259170"]

After my cute shark friend, I finished 44 Stormtroopers, 6 Probe Droids, a customizable Officer and Agent, and General Tagge. Super excited to play General Tagge, only so I can shout about excel spreadsheets whenever I play his command cards.

[gallery size="full" td_select_gallery_slide="slide" ids="259176,259174,259172"]

As a young child, Star Wars: The Force Unleashed was one of my favorite games, and I felt super inspired to paint my Stormtroopers as Triton Squad from the first few missions of the game.

[gallery size="full" td_select_gallery_slide="slide" ids="259178,259179,259177"]

Credit: dirtboi

Super happy with my progress this month, partly because of my participation in the Paintober Painting Challenge. 105 models completed from start to finish in the month of October. My brushes need a cigarette. See yall next month!

title: Board game show SPIEL Essen says "our team has not laughed" at $15,000 theft from exhibitor stand

On October 29, the UK Instagram account for the dart-throwing party game Tossit announced "we were robbed at [SPIEL] Essen", Europe's biggest board game convention, with goods and gear worth $15,650 (€14,000) taken between the close of the show on Sunday October 25 and the team returning to dismantle the booth on Monday. Tossit also claims that "instead of receiving practical help, we were met with laughter" by SPIEL Essen and venue staff - something that the convention denies.

SPIEL Essen is the most important event in the European board games industry, and arguably the world, a colossal convention where designers, publishers, and distributors strike business deals, while the general public knock elbows in their hunt for the best board games. Exhibiting is very costly, even before considering the risk of theft.

"On Sunday, October 25, 22:45hs, we left our stock at our booth to finish dismantling during the official dismantling hours", Tossit reports. "When we returned on Monday, October 26 8am, €14,000 worth of products and equipment were gone". Even "the tools we had stored inside our stand furniture were gone, leaving us without the equipment we needed to dismantle."

The studio adds that when it reported the theft to "representatives of SPIEL Essen and Messe Essen" - the exhibition venue where the convention takes place - "instead of receiving practical help, we were met with laughter".

It adds that "we were told there was no continuous camera surveillance inside the halls", and it is left with questions about "who had access overnight? What security measures were in place?"

Tossit states that "on our flight home, we met other exhibitors who told us they had also been robbed". Reviewing the comments to Tossit's post, Wargamer found three further claims from tabletop companies who state they had been stolen from when exhibiting at Essen this year or previously:

  • Retailer 'The Rolling Inn' reports a theft of €4,000 this year, adding "The guard mocked us yelling we have to go".
  • Board game maker Dicecoalitiongames reports "the exact same thing happened to us in 2025".
  • Tabletop marketer Dinasaidso says "We had this happen the last three years and decided to not go this year as honestly the costs are high enough as it is".

SPIEL Essen has already replied to Tossit's original post using its official Instagram account, stating:

"We take every allegation of theft very seriously. We are already in direct contact with the exhibitor and Messe Essen to clarify the facts of the matter, and the police have already been notified. Our team has taken the situation seriously at all times and, above all, has not laughed at any of the parties involved. Since the matter is currently under investigation, we ask for your understanding that we cannot comment further on this publicly on social media."

Wargamer has reached out to the media team at SPIEL Essen to ask for any updates, but at press time we haven't received a response. We will update you as soon as we hear anything.

We have, however, had a response from Messe Essen, the massive exhibition centre where SPIEL takes place. Press team leader Tom Kraayvanger explains the venue's stance:

"Messe Essen is responsible for general site security, securing buildings and access points, and fire safety," but "responsibility for securing individual exhibition stands and the goods and items displayed there lies with the respective exhibitors".

Messe provides an "option of booking professional stand security services" for exhibitors, which "includes corresponding insurance coverage".

Kraayvanger states that "the risk of individual thefts unfortunately cannot be completely ruled out" during the dismantling phase of a large event. He emphasises the "logistical and organisational challenges" of dismantling 85,000 square meters of stands and display areas "within just 24 hours", during which "thousands of people are working on the exhibition grounds simultaneously", including "exhibitors, stand construction companies, logistics service providers, and technical personnel".

As for the video surveillance coverage of the halls, Kraayvanger states that Messe is taking into account "data protection requirements and the privacy rights of the many people present on the exhibition grounds during an event and its set-up and dismantling phases".

He adds that "when large numbers of people are moving goods, material and equipment at the same time, camera footage does not make it possible to distinguish between the legitimate removal of items and their unauthorized removal", so "comprehensive video surveillance could not guarantee complete protection against theft".

He notes that Messe is "not aware of any other comparable thefts in connection with SPIEL 2026", and does not comment on the conduct of representatives or the claims that Tossit.UK staff were laughed at. He does not directly address the fact that this theft apparently occurred overnight, not during the designated dismantling period.

If you're a designer who has experienced a major theft at this or other conventions, you can reach Wargamer via the official Wargamer Discord community.

Site editor Mollie Russell was on the ground at SPIEL Essen 2026, and has some rather more upbeat reports to share - a playtest of Greenwood, one of the hottest games from the show; her take on the best games and hidden gems from this year's show; and her experiences with Trench Crusade as a first time wargamer.

Yugioh banlist FAQ

What is the Yu Gi Oh banlist?

Yugioh TCG publisher Konami releases an updated version of the Yu Gi Oh banlist every few months. This lists all the restrictions on the cards you can include in constructed Yu Gi Oh! decks (and tells you when previously banned or restricted cards have been unbanned!)

The three restricted types in Yugioh banlist are:

  • Forbidden - This card cannot be used in your Main Deck, Extra Deck, or Side Deck.
  • Limited / Limited 1 - You can only have one copy of this card in your main Deck, Extra Deck, and Side Deck combined.
  • Semi-limited / Limited 2 - You can only have two copies of this card in your Main Deck, Extra Deck, and Side Deck combined.

There are separate banlists for the game's 'Advanced' format (which is used in Regional, National, and World Championship events) and the much looser 'Traditional' format. For example, many cards are Forbidden in Advanced, but only Limited in Traditional format.

Forbidden, Limited, and Semi-limited cards can be cards of any type, and the Yu Gi Oh banlist typically contains numerous Monster, Monster/Effect, Monster/Fusion, Monster/Link, Monster/Synchro, Monster/Xyz, Spell, and Trap type cards.

Why do Yugioh cards get banned?

As with all the best trading card games, the Yugioh TCG regularly releases new sets of cards to keep the game fresh and offer players new strategies, themes, and options for their decks. When players get their hands on the new cards,  they quickly discover the most powerful options, especially cards that create strong combo effects with existing or older cards. This is, of course, part of the fun!

However, it can lead to just a handful of decks becoming dominant, able to beat any other decks they face - and thus the game's overall scene (often called its 'meta') becomes very samey, as everyone is forced to play with similar decks and cards if they want to have a chance of winning games.

Konami generally tries to maintain competitive balance with the range of new cards it releases - but with a game as complex and high-powered as Yugioh, cards will always emerge that 'warp the meta' and generate bad player feedback.

These are the sorts of cards that end up getting banned - either Semi-Limited, Limited or Forbidden - because they:

  • Are inherently too powerful (normally in combat power).
  • Are part of a combo that is too powerful / too easy to win with.
  • Are too versatile in cancelling out, or 'shutting down' multiple other strategies.
  • Are likely to cause problems in one of the above ways, after an upcoming release joins the meta.

Are there any permanently banned Yugioh cards?

While there's no official status for a Yugioh card being banned forever, there are a few cards we expect will never return from the Forbidden zone, because the features that made them too powerful are only becoming more overpowered as time goes on.

Because matches of the Yugioh TCG can be dominated by extremely powerful, quick combo plays that can end the game very quickly, some of the most powerful banned cards tend to be ones that let you draw extra cards, or find exactly the cards you need from your deck, without a significant cost attached.

The three most prominent examples of these long banned cards are:

  • Pot of Greed (Spell card) Draw two cards.
  • Painful Choice (Spell card) Select five cards from your deck and show them to your opponent. They choose one card to add to your hand, and the rest go to your Graveyard.
  • Graceful Charity (Spell card) Draw three cards, then discard two cards.

What's the difference between the Yugioh TCG and OCG?

There are two separate forms of the Yu-Gi-Oh! card game: the Trading Card Game (TCG) - which is sold and played worldwide, with cards printed in English and several European languages - and the Official Card Game (OCG), which is only available in Japanese language, and played mainly in Japan.

The Japanese OCG has a different release schedule for new sets and products; it runs on slightly different tournament rules; it gets its own exclusive cards not available in the TCG; and it has its own separate banlist of Forbidden and Limited cards, which gets updated via its own Japanese language website.

It's a key difference from the Pokémon TCG, where the main differences between Japanese Pokémon cards and English ones are in the card designs, print quality, and release schedule, but the game rules are the same and there's no structural separation between the two.

And that's it for our complete guide to the official Yugioh TCG banlist - for now! If you want to trade hot takes and predictions for upcoming bans, or just hype about Yugioh and every other bangin' tabletop game on the planet, join us in the free Wargamer Discord community!
