title: The best MTG Commanders November 2026
content:
The Commander is the legendary creature that leads your other 99 cards into battle in games of EDH: they dictate the colors you can include in your deck, and shape your overall strategy. If you're shopping for new options, our tried-and-tested guide to the best MTG commanders recommends plenty that reliably secure wins and are extremely fun to play.

Wizards of the Coast introduces more legendary creatures with each year of new MTG sets, but this guide will help you keep up with the latest releases and meta shifts. If you want to get really competitive, you'll be better served by our dedicated cEDH tier list. Or, if you're just starting out with this format, we'd recommend starting out with MTG commander precon decks instead.

Latest MTG commanders news in November

The list below covers the best MTG commanders that have already been released. However, spoiler season shows us spicy new options long before they go to print. If you want the most up-to-date MTG commander announcements, here's a brief summary of November's biggest news.

Star Trek spoiler season is upon us, ahead of the new set's launch on November 13. For commander players, all eyes are on the new Borg Queen precon and her habit of assimilating creatures from other players' decks.

Beyond this, the big announcements have all been Marvel-flavored. Four Darkhold Destiny commander decks have been confirmed for next year's Universes Beyond set. Among those spoilers, we're most intrigued by Gargantos, the Endbringer, who can get suitably massive depsite its 0/0 statline.

After Darkhold, we know that all future releases will come with four commander decks. That's a huge amount of choice in 2027!

Top commanders MTG:

  • Atraxa, Praetors' Voice
  • Edgar Markov
  • Vivi Ornitier
  • Teval, the Balanced Scale
  • Baylen, the Haymaker
  • The Necrobloom
  • Kenrith, The Returned King
  • Muldrotha, The Gravetide
  • Tymna The Weaver
  • The Gitrog Monster
  • Isshin, Two Heavens As One
  • Yuriko, the Tiger's Shadow
  • Sauron, The Dark Lord
  • The Ur Dragon
  • Kaalia Of The Vast
  • Lathril, Blade Of The Elves
  • Pantlaza, Sun Favored
  • Shroofus Sproutshire
  • Atraxa, Grand Unifier

Atraxa, Praetors' Voice

While not quite the dominant force she was in 2016, Atraxa, Praetors' Voice still makes for a top commander. Her proliferate ability opens up all kinds of avenues and has only gotten more flexible as Wizards experiments with new types of counters like shield and stun.

Atraxa is a really great commander to experiment with because her ability and color identity mean you can explore about six different themes. You could make a pretty standard +1/+1 counter deck, or go the opposite route with -1/-1 counters. You could be really unpleasant and run with poison counters, or create a superfriends deck full of planeswalkers.Whatever route you go, you're probably going to want more effects that proliferate, so cards like Ezuri, Stalker of Spheres and Tekuthal, Inquiry Dominus are a perfect fit. They also often lend themselves to a Phyrexian theme!

Game Changers for Atraxa, Praetor's Voice

  • Fierce Guardianship
  • Force of Will

Edgar Markov

The Commander 2017 set was all about tribal decks, each focused on a single creature type: cats, wizards, dragons, and vampires. Edgar Markov led the cats - no, sorry, the vampires deck - and quickly rose to the status of top commander. While the card got horribly pricey as a result, a reprint in Innistrad Remastered has made him a little less silly to buy.

With the ability to create a swarm of little nippers, then pump them up each time he attacks, Edgar naturally works best in a horde-style deck that can swiftly overwhelm opponents. Mardu colors give you access to all the top removal cards, and best of all, Edgar's eminence ability makes him useful from the command zone, where he can churn out mini-mes in safety.

You then need stuff to do with all your vampire tokens, like buffing them up or sacrificing them for card draw with Skullclamp and draining your opponent with Blood Artist.

Game Changers for Edgar Markov

  • Braids, Cabal Minion

Vivi Ornitier

MTG's Final Fantasy set was stuffed with legendary creatures, but Vivi Ornitier is the real standout for Commander players. He grows more powerful every time you cast a non-creature spell, and that power in turn fuels an incredibly versatile mana-making ability.

Vivi can be hard to keep in play due to his notoriety (he did terrible things in Standard) but on the bright side, his mana cost is so low that it shouldn't be too hard to bring him back. Keep him on the board long enough, and Vivi becomes a powerful attacker in his own right, but his real value lies in the win conditions you can create with the killer combination of free mana and pinging. A Curiosity-type card also makes this guy a card draw machine.

With Vivi, your game plan might be a spellslinger or storm build - setting up until the perfect turn allows you to combo off. Alternatively, you could go all in on pingers, and aim to whittle your opponents down with a million tiny cuts.

Game Changers for Vivi

  • Cyclonic Rift
  • Mystical Tutor
  • Rhystic Study

Teval, the Balanced Scale

Teval, the Balanced Scale offers fantastic value, especially for a precon commander. This spicy spirit dragon has seen its popularity soar since Tarkir: Dragonstorm, and no wonder. It's a consistent source of land and tokens whose self-mill strategies synergize with a variety of decks.

Obviously, a straightforward graveyard deck is the first place to go. You want cards entering and leaving your graveyard as often as possible to trigger Teval's ability. After that though, you could consider a lands-matter sub-theme, playing multiple lands a turn to stack up the triggers. You could look to get the most from your tokens with zombie tribal cards too.

Your biggest problem will be defending Teval, who has no protection against removal, will suffer when cards are exiled, and who must constantly jump into the fray of battle.

Gamechangers for Teval

  • Force of Will
  • Fierce Guardianship
  • Gifts Ungiven

Baylen, the Haymaker

If you love using tokens, Baylen, the Haymaker might just be the best commander in all of Magic: The Gathering history, but he has surprising depth - this isn't just your typical go-wide tokens leader.

You wouldn't necessarily know that from the first step of your gameplan though: you begin by amassing a token army. They don't all have to be creatures, you can use treasure or food as well. But after this step is where the rabbit is flexible.

If you want to win with commander damage, you can tap your tokens to buff Baylen up with counters and swing for lethal. He turns four tokens into three +1/+1 counters, so even without built-in protection, this is very doable.

Alternatively, you can use your tokens for mana and card draw. That lets you dig through your deck and cast other key pieces that will help you convert tokens into victory.

I'll lastly add that there are few better commanders to pick for an Hare Apparent deck, if you just want to overwhelm your foes with a lupine legion.

Gamechangers for Baylen

  • Smothering Tithe
  • Biorhythm
  • Aura Shards

The Necrobloom

The Necrobloom is easy for opponents to underestimate. On its early turns, it doesn't seem to achieve much - play a land, fetch a land, create a puny plant token. However, if left undisturbed for long enough, it's landfall antics will start to cause serious problems.

As soon as seven types of land are under your control, you can start building a zombie army, all while blocking with your chunky commander their numerous plant buddies. Dredge is on hand to bring back any crucial lands, and it opens up plenty of interactions that keep The Necrobloom's tokens-and-landfall schtick feeling interesting.

Mass land-reanimation is particularly deadly in this deck, creating a huge horde that has to be dealt with in one turn cycle, else it's game over.

Gamechangers for the Necrobloom

  • Field of the Dead
  • Crop Rotation

Kenrith, The Returned King

Five-color commanders are some of the strongest because they allow you to use any card in the game. That means ultimate flexibility. As a result, they're a little controversial, since many lend themselves to less focused strategies and decks, where you just want to cram in all the best cards in your collection.

But we think that's as valid a playstyle as any - and it's hard to pass up jack-of-all-trades commanders when they're as good as Kenrith, the Returned King. Kenrith shines because all of his abilities are useful, and some are invaluable. You only need white mana to cast him, so you can have him out on the field and gradually unlock new abilities as you play new lands.

He's a top commander for those still learning how to play Magic The Gathering's most popular format, since you can experiment to your heart's content, and it's hard to go too wrong. Synergy is not required - just brute strength!

Gamechangers for Kenrith

  • Coalition Victory
  • Gifts Ungiven
  • Fierce Guardianship

Muldrotha, The Gravetide

Do you hate it when your opponents blow up your stuff? Then Muldrotha, the Gravetide is the top commander for you. Allowing you to play one card of each permanent type from your graveyard each and every turn, this noxious elemental turns your graveyard into an extension of your hand.

Unfortunately, with a high cost and incredible ability, Muldrotha is one of those commanders that attracts removal like a magnet. On the bright side, her Sultai colors (black, green and blue) give you access to a ton of power outside of her own impressive strength, including excellent creatures, removal, and card draw.

And when you do manage to protect her for long enough to make good use of her resurrection powers, your opponents are going to have a bad time.

Gamechangers for Muldrotha

  • Gifts Ungiven
  • Intuition
  • Fierce Guardianship

Tymna The Weaver

Tymna the Weaver may not look like much from the outset - sure, she draws cards when you hit people, whatever. But never underestimate the power of friendship. Tymna is a top commander choice because she has the Partner ability, which - like Tymna herself - was introduced in the Commander 2016 set. That means you can pair her up with any legendary creature that also has 'Partner' to give them joint leadership of your commander deck.

Two commanders are better than one, since they unlock new card options and new synergies, as well as ensuring you always have a creature to play out. Tymna makes this list simply because she's one of the most versatile creatures with the Partner ability. The card draw she provides will be valuable, whatever strategy you're going for.

Tymna the Weave is most often paired up with the merfolk card Thrasios, Triton Hero. That's because this combination gives you access to four colors and two commanders with generically powerful abilities. They don't make Partners like this anymore, and for good reason.

Gamechangers for Tymna

  • Thassa's Oracle
  • Orcish Bowmasters

The Gitrog Monster

A froggy chap with a winning smile, The Gitrog Monster has a series of unique, versatile abilities that make for a powerful MTG commander. It lets you play more lands, allowing for copious ramping, and you get to draw cards each time you put lands in the graveyard.

Cards like Crucible of Worlds will help you bring valuable lands back to the battlefield so you can sacrifice them again and again for endless utility. Even a simple Evolving Wilds can be extremely useful for Gitrog.

Whether you're using discard outlets or sacrificing lands, there's plenty of ways to generate absurd value with this top commander. You can also abuse infinite combos, which makes The Gitrog Monster a viable combo deck in cEDH.

Gamechangers for the Gitrog Monster

  • Crop Rotation
  • Field of the Dead
  • Glacial Chasm

Isshin, Two Heavens As One

Isshin, Two Heavens as One has just one simple ability, but its elegance and simplicity belies its power. This high tech samurai doubles up all your attack triggers, letting you generate absurd value whenever you swing at your opponents.

Not the best commander for anyone who likes playing a slower, defensive game, Isshin wants you to strike hard and strike fast. While all Isshin decks want to attack, this is another commander that you can build in a few ways, as there are loads of strong creature cards to choose from, and plenty of room for building up subthemes.

Even better, his very affordable mana cost means you don't have to worry too much about removal spells, as you can play Isshin, Two Heavens as One several times without it becoming too taxing.

Gamechangers for Isshin

  • The One Ring
  • Jeska's Will
  • Teferi's Protection

Yuriko, the Tiger's Shadow

If you like ninjas, then Magic: The Gathering has a brilliant commander option. With Yuriko, the Tiger's Shadow, your whole deal is striking with low-cost, evasive creatures, then launching your commander into play with ninjitsu, and reaping the rewards: plenty of card draw, and plenty of pain.

The best thing about Yuriko is, as long as you have an unblocked creature, you can always get her into play for two mana. This is huge. It means no matter how many times your opponents deal with your commander, it's always a threat.

The rest of your deck is not so resilient to a board wipe - and a board wipe can seriously set you back, though you can usually hold up a counterspell or two to protect your ninja army. Yuriko makes for a top budget commander deck too - little unblockable guys don't tend to cost too much.

Gamechangers for a Yuriko deck

  • Force of Will
  • Consecrated Sphinx
  • Cyclonic Rift

Sauron, The Dark Lord

A six-cost commander in Grixis, a color combo not exactly known for ramp, is a tough sell. However, if you can hang on and play Sauron, the Dark Lord, you're all set to have a great time. He's a self-fueling engine.

Once Sauron comes down, he starts to roll an unstoppable boulder at your opponent. No one wants to pay the ward cost to get rid of him, and every time anyone casts a spell, you get another Amass trigger.

Soon, your Orcs will be enormous, something on your board will be very hard to block, and you'll be drawing several cards a turn. Sauron works great with several cards from the Lord of the Rings set, which have a very high power level. And you can bring in all the old Amass cards from War of the Spark, too.

He can also reliably pitch your hand into your graveyard, which can make a good setup for graveyard strategies - whether you're trying to get an Underworld Breach / Lion's Eye Diamond loop going for a combo, or just want to reanimate something huge.

Gamechangers for a Sauron deck

  • Demonic Tutor
  • Lion's Eye Diamond
  • Underworld Breach

The Ur Dragon

The Ur Dragon offers a simple strategy, but it's still powerful enough to stampede casual commander tables (and steal a few more competitive wins, too). Its Eminence keyword means that, whether this card is on the battlefield or not, all your MTG dragons are one mana cheaper. The plan should be clear from here - fill your deck with huge, hard-hitting fliers and let rip.

The Ur Dragon is very expensive to get on the battlefield. However, it's a 10/10 flyer that allows you to draw cards equal to the number of your attacking dragons. Even better, you can then place a permanent from your hand onto the battlefield for free.

There are plenty of cards that synergize with The Ur Dragon's matter-of-fact battle plan. Prioritize those that give you extra benefits for playing dragons onto the battlefield or that can make these mana-hungry creatures even cheaper. You'll also need a solid ramp plan if you want your enormous dragons to get off the ground.

Gamechangers for The Ur Dragon

  • Mana Vault
  • Ancient Tomb
  • Chrome Mox

Kaalia Of The Vast

Kaalia of the Vast has been considered a top commander almost since the format's inception. Even today, this card's powers are impressive. Kaalia is a four-cost Mardu commander with flying and the ability to add a card from your hand to the battlefield whenever she attacks. That card must be an Angel, Demon, or Dragon creature, and it's automatically tapped and attacking along with Kaalia.

This is a ferociously fast way to cheat flying threats onto the field. If you can give Kaalia haste, your chosen commander can start handing out freebies as early as turn four. Lightning Greaves, Swiftwood Boots, and Dragon Tempest are your friend here.

Naturally, you'll want a deck full of angels, demons, and dragons to back Kaalia up. You should also leave space for problem-solving cards. Kaalia is a veteran of the competitive commander scene, so you can expect many players to have a game plan when she shows up - removal, removal, and removal.

Gamechangers for a Kaalia of the Vast deck

  • Teferi's Protection
  • Demonic Tutor
  • Imperial Seal


Lathril, Blade Of The Elves

As one of the oldest and best-established creature types in all of Magic: The Gathering, elves have long been a super powerful tribe. There's just been so much time for Wizards to print good elves, and there are now so many of them standing around pouting and hugging trees that it's almost too easy to make a strong elves deck. Just find the cards with the pointy ears and chuck a bunch in.

Lathril, Blade of the Elves is a Kaldheim commander who provides a nice bit of edge for elves decks by adding black to their color identity. This top commander also gives you a powerful new win condition, letting you use your elvish army to drain your opponents for huge chunks of life.

Lathril gives you plenty of options. You can build her to be a classic green elves deck, which ramps up quickly to a critical mass of creatures and then pulls out one of umpteen win conditions. But you can also create a combo style deck that relies on untappers to build up infinite mana, or uses them with Lathril herself to close out the game.

Gamechangers for Lathril

  • Natural Order
  • Survival of the Fittest
  • Gaea's Cradle

Pantlaza, Sun-Favored

Open the door, get on the floor, and prepare to walk the dinosaur, with one of the most popular MTG commanders of recent years. There's a good reason Pantlaza Sun-Favored sees so much play. Coming out of one of the best precon decks ever released, this raptor is a top commander choice if you just want to throw around some big stompy dinosaurs.

Pantlaza's Discover ability means that each dinosaur you cast has the potential to trigger a cascade, letting you fetch up one or potentially more other random dinosaurs from your deck (worst case scenario you hit a mana rock or something). It feels great to start a turn with just your commander on board, and end it with a herd of colossal reptiles whose approaching roars tell your opponents that you are very much the threat. Just make sure you pack enough ramp!

The randomness of this ability might be frustrating to some, but for others it'll ensure their deck always feels fresh.

Gamechangers for Pantlaza

  • Teferi's Protection
  • Farewell
  • Gaea's Cradle

Shroofus Sproutsire

We're not sure if Shroofus Sproutsire truly deserves to be on a list of all-time top commanders, but we've included him as an added extra because we couldn't bear to upset the lil' guy. He's certainly one of the best Jumpstart 2025 Commanders at any rate.

You're always going to have to put a bit of work in to land a hit with this commander, but once you get the ball rolling it's going to move very very fast. While he'd probably work better as Slimefoot's right hand man, this creature will feel like having Scute Swarm in your command zone.

Gamechangers for Shroofus Sproutshire

  • Gaea's Cradle
  • Natural Order
  • Seedborn Muse

Atraxa, Grand Unifier

Alright, Atraxa, Grand Unifier comes with an eye-watering mana cost, and it doesn't have the explosive proliferate powers of our other favored Atraxa commander. However, Grand Unifier offers heaps of power and versatility.

This is a mighty 7/7 commander with flying, vigilance, deathtouch, and lifelink. If you can keep Atraxa in play, it'll obliterate opposing forces, dole out enormous chunks of commander damage, and keep you well-defended in the meantime.

Perhaps more important is Atraxa's enters-the-battlefield ability. This allows you to reveal ten cards from the top of your library. For each card type among those, you can put one card of each revealed type into your hand. The rest go on the bottom of your library in a random order.

This is a commander with fairly generic powers that can feel a bit 'jack of all trades, master of none'. However, this also makes Atraxa suitable for a variety of deck types, from Blink to Phyrexian Typal.

Gamechangers for Atraxa, Grand Unifier

  • Thassa's Oracle
  • Grand Arbiter Augustin IV
  • Force of Will

Thorin, King of Durin's Folk

One of our recent favorites, Thorin, King of Durin's Folk is the new hot dwarf on the block. Lovers of typal decks, stuffed to the brim with Treasure and Equipment, are in for a treat. Thorin creates a Treasure token whenever he or another Dwarf enters, and he gives other Dwarves +1/+1 for each artifact token you control.

It's a simple formula: spam tokens, buff Dwarves, profit. Despite its simplicity, it's tremendous fun to build and play. There are plenty of Dwarves who can be their own source of artifact tokens, including obvious champion Magda.

Gamechangers for Thorin, King of Durin's Folk

  • Magda, Brazen Outlaw
  • Gloin, Dwarf Emissary
  • Smaug the Magnificent

Brewing a new deck and need to troubleshoot it? Or just want to share your latest creation? We're always keen to find out what nerds are up to in the Wargamer Discord community. And to keep up to date with the latest news and features about everything tabletop, make sure you're subscribed to the Wargamer newsletter.

Over the game's 33-year history, Wizards of the Coast has released 233 card collections, better known as MTG sets. With thousands of cards behind us, and even more approaching, that's a lot of sets to track. To help you stay up-to-date, we've put together a complete list of all Magic: The Gathering sets in order.

Because everybody wants to know what's new, we start with the up-and-comers and the most recent sets released. After that, our total of 233 counts all Core, Standard Expansion, Supplemental, Starter, Compilation sets since 1993, as well as the jokey 'Un-Sets', one-and-done Box Sets, Commander Sets, and miscellaneous multiplayer products.

Since Commander is such a big part of the game, we've also copied out all the Commander precons and other commander products into a separate list . We haven't counted digital-only Alchemy sets, but there are some MTGO exclusive sets in here!

For info on just the latest sets, you can find more drilled-down detail in our MTG release schedule guide. You can also hop to our FAQ segment below for some helpful facts and trivia about the history of Magic: The Gathering sets.

MTG Commander sets

From 2011 to 2019, Wizards of the Coast released Commander decks and other products just once per year. Since May 15 2020, the firm has released batches of precons parallel to new mainline Magic sets. Although they share the set's theme and narrative, they have their own set code and set symbol.

Magic: The Gathering sets FAQ

Above are all the sets, right back to the very beginnings of Magic: The Gathering, but if you're new to the game, some more info might be in order. Here's the lowdown on how these releases work.

What are MTG sets?

Most Magic: The Gathering sets aren't individual boxed products on a shelf, like Lego sets or Warhammer 40k box sets. Instead, an MTG set is a distinct, named new collection of MTG cards released and added to the game's existing pool of playable cards.

Depending on the type, each set will normally have its own theme, either based around a particular fictional setting in the lore, or perhaps tailored to one particular mode of play, like the Commander or Modern formats.

What are the types of MTG sets?

We've created several categories to make our list of every MTG set easier to peruse. Here's what those terms mean:

  • Expansion: These are the regular Magic: The Gathering sets, legal in Standard, and released at regular intervals throughout the year.
  • Compilation: These are reprint sets with no new cards. Often these contain a compilation of cards set on the same plane.
  • Un-set: These are joke sets with cards that have weird, wacky effects. Cards from these sets usually have silver borders and are not been legal in other formats.
  • Universes Beyond set: One of Magic: The Gathering's many crossover sets. Now that MTG Universes Beyond sets are Standard-legal, this category has merged with regular expansions somewhat.
  • Core set: Beginner-friendly sets that are Standard legal - these have been canceled and reintroduced several times.
  • Box set: Sets with a predetermined batch of cards, where what you get is not randomized.
  • Supplemental set: A catch-all category for MTG sets that don't fall into one of the above categories. These include many of WotC's experiments over the years, as well as expansions built for specific formats other than Standard.

When do new MTG sets come out on MTG Arena?

Currently, every new Standard set releases on MTG Arena a few days before the physical products are available in stores. 

Most new Standard sets also herald an Alchemy release of about 25-30 Arena-only cards that are not produced in physical form. These cards are specially designed to work best in the digital format. They often include mechanics that would be impractical in regular Magic, such as summoning random creatures from your deck, creating new cards, or permanently altering others.

How many cards are in each MTG set?

Each new MTG set normally contains somewhere between 200 and 300 cards. The selection almost always includes a mixture of brand new cards (where the card name, in-game rules, and art are all new) and 'reprints' (new versions of existing popular cards, which keep the same name and rules, but may feature new artwork and sometimes updated wording).

What is the biggest MTG set ever released?

The biggest single MTG set ever released was the Fifth Edition core set in 1997, which had 449 new cards in total, including 20 Basic Lands.

Other massive sets from the early era of Magic include its immediate predecessor, 1995's Fourth Edition core set, with 363 cards; 1996's Mirage, with 350, and 1997's Tempest, which also added 350 cards to the game.

Sets started becoming smaller during the aughts, although 2007's  Lorwyn bucked the trend with a mighty 301 cards.

What is the smallest MTG set ever released?

The smallest MTG set of all time, by total number of cards, is technically 2023's March of the Machine: Aftermath, with just 50 new cards. But, if we discount that as merely a mini add-on to the 291-card March of the Machine, the smallest legitimate set is Arabian Nights, the very first 'expansion' set, released in December 1993 with just 92 cards.

Oh, you meant the actual smallest cards? That honor is held by the Worlds Smallest Magic: The Gathering Exclusive Collector Set pictured above - a painfully adorable, now sadly discontinued joke product that included two itsy-bitsy duel decks composed of downsized, 1.2 x 1.8 inch cards, as well as teeny weeny spindown dice.

How many MTG sets are released each year?

Currently, Wizards of the Coast releases between six and ten MTG sets per year. We get three to four full 'Standard' sets annually (about one every three months) and a varying mix of smaller sets - usually focused on specific formats, or revisiting a popular past setting with additional cards.

According to comments from Magic's head designer Mark Rosewater in May 2026, the "new normal" from next year onwards will be a "three and three" split between Universes Beyond crossover sets (like Lord of the Rings and Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles) and sets based in Magic's own fiction (like Lorwyn Eclipsed and  Secrets of Strixhaven).

In addition, Wizards releases what it calls 'Secret Lair drops', which are much smaller, limited edition print runs of specially designed cards aimed at collectors - often themed around franchises, fandoms, or art styles outside of Magic.

What products come with each MTG set?

Every time a new MTG set is released, Wizards of the Coast produces a range of different products containing the new cards, in different configurations, for various types of players.

Currently, every main MTG set releases with:

  • Play boosters - packs of 14 random cards including at least one Rare or Mythic Rare.
  • Collector boosters - packs of 15 random cards including 4-5 guaranteed Rares and Mythic Rares, plus special art cards.
  • Bundles - a mixed box containing 9 play boosters, 30 land cards, and accessories like tokens and counters.
  • Commander decks - pre-built 100-card decks for the Commander (EDH) game format. Each set normally has between two and four of these, also called Commander 'precons' (short for preconstructed decks).
  • Prerelease pack - A box sold at prerelease events, with six Play boosters, one promo card (a foil Rare or Mythic Rare stamped with the year), a deck box, an Arena code, and a spindown die with the set symbol.

What are the most popular MTG sets?

The answer depends a lot on personal taste, but there is a way to generally feel out which sets are most loved - and that's money. According to Hasbro, the best-selling MTG set of all time is Final Fantasy. Second and third place also go to Universes Beyond sets, with MTG Lord of the Rings following Final Fantasy, and Avatar: The Last Airbender bringing up the rear.

If you'd like to debate which of these sets is truly best, you've got a willing audience over in the Wargamer Discord - and to stay informed about upcoming releases, subscribe to the Wargamer newsletter.

title: MTG Arena codes for November 2026
content:
MTG Arena codes are an essential, mostly free kick-start for your digital collection, unlocking new Magic: The Gathering cards, booster packs, XP, and cosmetic items like card sleeves, avatars, and more. Read on to find all working MTGA codes in 2026, as well as full instructions on how to redeem promo codes on PC and mobile.

Each month, we trawl Wizards' announcements about new MTG sets to update this list (if you want more details on said sets, check out the linked guide, or this one on the MTG release schedule). We'll tell you which codes currently work; which have expired; and which brand-new codes have sprung up for the game. The good news is that you can still unlock free cards to boost your decks.

Here's how to get MTGA codes:

  • All free MTG Arena codes in November 2026
  • Unlock the cabbage companion
  • MTG Arena rewards
  • How to redeem MTG Arena codes
  • Where to find more MTGA codes
  • All expired MTGA codes

All free MTG Arena codes in November 2026

For the first time in ages, there actually are MTG Arena codes to be used (for now, at least!) A chain of riddles, released alongside the Hobbit set, will win you some cards, card styles and a unique avatar.

Originally, this promo was expected to end around August 27, but as of our latest test on Tuesday, October 1, it still works! We can't be sure how long for, though, so if you want your Bilbo goodies, hurry up! Here's what to do:

Right now, if you check your inbox, you'll find a riddle. Input the answer as an MTG Arena code in the store to unlock a reward and the next riddle. Keep going until you've answered all eight, then create a deck with all eight of the cards you just unlocked. 

It doesn't have to be legal, or even have the correct number of cards, so just plonk them all in and save it. Name the deck 'Riddles in the Dark', and you'll receive a Bilbo avatar.

If you want to try to solve the riddles yourself, exit this page right now. We're assuming you're here for the answers, which you'll find below.

  • Riddle #1: Mountain (The Mountain-king's Return card and borderless card style)
  • Riddle #2: Teeth (Gnashing of Teeth card and borderless card style)
  • Riddle #3: Wind (Velvetwing Butterflies card and borderless card style)
  • Riddle #4: Darkness (Gathering of Darkness card and borderless card style)
  • Riddle #5: Egg (Well-Worn Spatula card and borderless card style)
  • Riddle #6: Fish (Lake-town Mariners card and borderless card style)
  • Riddle #7: Time (Stone by Sunlight card and borderless card style)
  • Riddle #8: Precious (My Precious rare card and borderless card style)

In case you skimmed the bit above, you now need to make a deck called Riddles in the Dark with all eight of these cards to unlock the final reward.

Unlock the cabbage companion

Would you like to have a high fidelity cabbage for your companion? Of course you would! This nutritious friend is available as a free easter egg, added to celebrate the MTG Avatar: The Last Airbender set in 2025. You can unlock it by playing any matched game on the Avatar battlefield, and clicking on the Cabbage Merchant's cart until it explodes. Do this and you'll be rewarded with your very own cabbage.

Can't find the cart? It's at the top of the battlefield, just to the left of your opponent's profile picture.

Is the cabbage companion better than the beachball or the pet rock? That's for you to judge.

MTG Arena rewards

These days, Wizards hands out free booster packs as MTG Arena rewards to celebrate the release of new sets. These arrive directly in your in-game inbox without the need to redeem a code. Plus, new players who complete the how to play tutorial are greeted with a whole stack of reward packs to crack open from the last couple of years' worth of sets (plus a selection of variant land cards to use).

How to redeem MTG Arena codes

There are two ways to redeem MTG Arena codes on PC, and both are dead easy - just pick your method below and follow our step-by-step guide.

How to redeem codes in the Arena client

The most common and simplest way to cash in your codes is directly inside the MTG Arena client. Here's how to do it:

1. Open up the game on PC and click on the 'Store' tab at the top of the page.

2. You'll see a small oval text box in the top right corner, with 'Redeem Code' written inside (we've highlighted it in red in the picture above).

3. Copy your code into the box and hit enter.

4. Your reward automatically appears in your account!

How to redeem codes via your Wizards account

If you'd rather not boot up the game, you can also redeem codes by entering them into your Wizards of the Coast account page. Here's how you do this:

1. Log in using your MTG Arena details, and on the right-hand side of your account dashboard, you'll find a nice, big 'Redeem a code' box.

2. Paste the code inside and click 'Redeem'.

3. The goods will appear in your account next time you log in to the Arena game client.

How to redeem MTGA codes on mobile

If you're primarily a mobile MTGA player and want to redeem codes on your phone, the process can feel a bit more convoluted, because - frustratingly - there's still no way to redeem codes directly through the iOS and Android versions of the game.

The main way to get the job done is simply via mobile web, with the following steps:

  1. Log in to your Wizards account via your mobile browser.
  2. Scroll down to the 'Redeem a Code' box as shown in the image above.
  3. Enter your code, and click 'Redeem'.
  4. Your rewards will show up next time you log into the game.

If everything's worked correctly, you'll see a little green message pop up that reads "Code redeemed successfully", as seen above.

However, if you really want to make things difficult for yourself, you can access that same account-based process from within the MTG Arena mobile client. We don't recommend it, though, because it's janky as all hell - it's far easier just to hop over to your mobile browser and do it there.

Where to find more MTGA codes

If you've already used all the free codes available, and still want to expand your collection of planeswalkers, creatures, and fancy land cosmetics, there are a few other places where you can sometimes get your hands on more MTGA codes to redeem. You can do this either by buying select Magic products that include Arena freebies, or else staying alert for new promo codes and other fans' unused codes shared online.

The main options to try are:

  • Physical Magic: The Gathering products
  • Social media giveaways and competitions
  • Promo codes from local game stores
  • MTG Arena Twitch Prime codes

Physical Magic: The Gathering products

Unlike the Pokémon TCG, not every sealed pack of Magic cards comes with a digital unlock code included - but some physical MTG products do give you a code into the bargain, to grow your digital collection as well as your cardboard mountain. There are three types of products you can buy for this.

Prerelease kits

Wizards of the Coast launches each new Magic: The Gathering set with a pre-release event focused on in-person games in local game stores, selling Prerelease kits of six brand new boosters.

Since 2025, these prerelease kits have no longer included MTG Arena codes packed in the box. Instead, you'll register your Arena account when you attend the pre-release event at a physical store, and your free boosters will appear in your account when you next log in.

MTG Arena Secret Lair codes

MTG Arena Secret Lair codes are found in Wizards of the Coast's limited edition, premium Secret Lair boxed sets of one-off collectible cards. The rewards vary, but usually, they unlock exclusive cards and cosmetics.

You can get some pretty sweet, limited edition skins, though - for example, if you bought the 'Warhammer Bundle' during the October 2023 Warhammer 40k Secret Lair, you got two codes, each good for ten premium card sleeves showing the 40k-ified versions of classic cards:

Beware, though - this is often the priciest way to find new codes. Each Secret Lair 'drop' can cost anything from $20 to several hundred bucks. We only recommend going this way if you really want the physical cards your codes will come bundled with.

Social media giveaways and competitions

If you're a social media-savvy Magic fan, another way to nab a cheeky extra code is through giveaways or competitions run by major MTG content creators, influencers, or simply kind-hearted fans sharing codes they don't need or want for themselves.

MTGA Codes, a retail website that collects unwanted and unused Arena codes and sells them directly online, regularly runs such giveaways to drive engagement on its Twitter account (@MTGA_CODES).

There's no way to know when such giveaways will take place, or exactly who's going to be doing them - but we can recommend a few creators you should follow just for regular, great content and commentary on Magic and Arena, who have been known to give away MTGA codes in the past:

It's not all the time, but Wizards of the Coast occasionally creates special MTG Arena codes as part of promoting in-person Magic play through bricks-and-mortar local game stores (LGS). Most recently, it did this via its 'Friday Night Magic At Home' campaign, aimed at helping stores keep regular play events going during Covid lockdowns in 2020.

This isn't a regular occurrence, though, and it's entirely dependent on Wizards' ongoing strategy for working with game stores - if you're angling for extra codes, we'd recommend checking in with the staff at your LGS to see if there's anything on offer.

MTG Arena Twitch Prime codes

In the past, Wizards of the Coast has collaborated with other big brands to offer MTG Arena promo codes as a bonus for their subscribers - and, back in 2019, it gave away free unlock codes as a benefit for the Twitch Prime service (now merged with Amazon Prime Gaming).

All you had to do to get the code was sign into your Twitch Prime account, check the 'Loot' section, click on 'claim', and it would generate a code for you to redeem directly in the Arena client.

Sadly, we haven't seen any more new MTGA codes come through this service in the years since - but there's always a chance, so if you're constantly on the hunt for fresh codes, it's worth periodically checking in on your Prime Gaming account (there's also a bunch of free videogame downloads and other goodies there, of course).

Naturally, we'll also update this guide the moment we see any new MTG Arena unlockables pop up on the platform.

title: [40k] Weekend Update: November 2, 2026
content:
In our Weekend Update series, we cover the big events and stories that are happening each week in wargames, so you can stay updated and informed every week. The 40k side will be mostly covered by me, Isaac Terada, while Dan “Swiftblade” Richardson covers the non-40k side of event coverage and news. 

Talavera Caps Off Weekend Big for Teams, Light for Singles

October ended with a surprising weekend that held only a single qualifying event in our sample - we typically only look at events with 5+ rounds and 28 players when we define our GT+ events - with only a single qualifying singles event for the weekend. Instead competitive 40k was dominated by teams events, headlined by the Talavera GT, a massive, 804-player teams event held in Talavera de la Reina, Spain, which marked the largest teams event of the year. This skew's the week's stats a little bit when it comes to understanding shifts in the meta, but you can rest assured that bikes and land speeders were still major factors globally.

Speaking of teams events...

Wargames Adictos Wins Year's Largest Teams Event

It was a particularly big weekend for six-man teams events, with Talavera and Super 6 both offering opportunities for teams of 6 to square off. The largest of these - and the year's biggest teams event (and also in contention for the year's biggest event) - was in Talavera, with 804 players split among 134 teams of six. The event itself was six rounds, leading to four undefeated teams at the end of the weekend, though ultimately Team Wargames Adictos won on points with a least featuring World Eaters (Recon), Imperial Knights (Purge), Necrons (Priority), Dark Angels (T&H), Orks (Disruption), and Thousand Sons (Priority).

Congratulations to:

  •  Gonzalo "Raven" de La Moneda
  •  Juanma Joker
  •  Manu
  •  Marco Esteban
  •  Miguel Durá
  •  Terroxer El Rojo

for winning the event, with an additional acknowledgement for Team Euskadi, 3 Arpía, and Cónclave for finishing with undefeated records.

Team England Takes October Super 6’s Crown

The weekend's next largest teams event featured only a measly 144 players duking it out over five rounds with six-player teams. Team England won the event with a 5-0 record, edging out Team Morocco for the top spot.

Congrats to:

  • Danny Evison
  • Harley Scully
  • Mani Cheema
  • Mike Porter
  • Tony Chew
  • Will B

Xenofilerna Omega Wins TTT 2026

The weekend's third big European event, team Xenofilerna Omega won this five-round, four-man teams event featuring 96 players.

Congrats to:

  • Benjamin Hyvönen
  • Björn Eriksson
  • Jacob Edvinsson
  • Johan Edvinsson

黑石要塞 Wins the South China Open

The final large teams event of the weekend was the South China Open, another 6-man teams event with four rounds and 84 total players. Team 黑石要塞 (which I believe translates to “Blackstone Fortress”) won the event with a 3-1-1 record.

Congrats to:

  • Bill Zuda
  • eddy E
  • 杂耍 Z
  • 白给 Wade
  • 老陈 C
  • 萝卜 L

Dylan Cowan Wins Weekend's Largest Singles 40k Event

The lone qualifying singles event this past weekend was the Calling the Banners 2026 event in Coburg North, Australia. This 67-player, 5-round event was conquered by Dylan Cowan, who won the event piloting a Dark Angels Take and Hold List running Assault Brethren, Darkflight Pursuit, Stormlance Task Force, and a ton of Outriders and Land Speeders.

Funny Thing About Statistics…

Actually I think Deathwatch might be bad; no one even played them this weekend. Necrons also had a record low 26% win rate. Well, this might be because we tracked a single GT event this weekend of just 67 players. Tracking win rates in teams tends to throw off data since the pairings process can lead to some factions having unnaturally high or low win rates. Tune in next week where we will hopefully have much more relevant results to study.

The ITC Is Dead! Long Live the WGR!

The ITC has been an integral part of the 40K scene for a very long time, much longer then my personal 40K career. Players who have been following the scene will have noticed that the ITC changed hands a few years ago, moving from its previous owners at Frontline Gaming to Games Workshop as part of the new World Championships program. Earlier this year Games Workshop finally chose to scuttle the ITC, renaming the ranking system to the Warhammer Global Rankings. Over the weekend Best Coast Pairings put out a social post on Facebook alluding to new scoring in the new season, starting after this year's World Championships, though no changes appear to have been announced or planned at this time.

I am sure many people can remember a time where Games Workshop did not care about competitive 40K; those days are certainly gone and I am excited to see where they continue to grow in how they mange the 40K competitive scene.

Photo Credit: Mani Cheema

Player Focus: Mani Cheema

As the 2026 World Championships rapidly approach, we'll look at the top players on the WGR leaderboards to see who can have a chance to take home the crown. We already covered spots #1 and #3 over the past weeks so let’s look to spot #2. Mani Cheema is a veteran player well known in the UK scene and currently second in the ITC, with a top teams finish this past weekend at the Super 6s event. Mani previously won the World Championships in 2023 and I'd be shocked if he didn't make a deep run at the crown again this year. Mani is a jack-of-all trades player: You’ll never know what he might be on, though he's often seen running powered-armoured Chaos warriors, such as with this past weekend's Death Guard list.

Alongside our coverage of the what's-what of 40k each week, Dan “Swiftblade” Richardson joins us to provide some quick updates on the movers and shakers in the competitive scene of some of the other games we cover here at Tabletop Battles!

Khazalite Holds Clanshields - Credit Mildnorman

Khazalite Holds Release over the Weekend; Wave Two Up for Preorder

It’s been a dwarf-heavy episode over in the Mortal realms, as the new Khazalite Holds faction has been front and center for Age of Sigmar since its announcement at the big autumn preview. For excited fans who are eager to bring the classic dwarf look and feel to AoS, this weekend marks two notable occasions. First is the wide release of the new army box set for the Khazalite holds, which offers not only a wide array of Khazalite models but also give eager fans their first chance to get their hands on the new Battletome.

Normally, we see a bit of a gap between an army box release and the wide army release, but in the case of Khazalite Holds the second wave of releases is hot on the army box’s heels, as preorders will go live on November 7th. There is an impressive number of models releasing this weekend as well, with the entire range of the faction shown off during the preview all included with the big release wave, rather than coming in a more staggered release schedule that we’ve often seen in the past.

If you’re interested in the newest Duardin face in the Mortal Realms, check out our review of the new Khazalite Holds Battletome to learn more!

Rules Updates for Age of Sigmar and Kill Team

While Warhammer 40,000’s rules update release last week was awkwardly released in little bits over several days, fans of Kill Team and Age of Sigmar lucked out and had their rules updates all drop at once last week, providing much-needed clarifications and errata for both game systems.

In the Mortal Realms, the bulk of the changes focused on the Fyreslayers and the Sons of Behemat. For the Fyreslayers, the faction keywords were updated across the board to change out the faction keyword to Khazalite, since the fiery-haired Duardin faction will be rolled into the upcoming Khazalite Holds faction, as well as updating how grudge token work in their regiment of renown. Regiments are also the main focus of the Behemat update, which introduces the new option for their Regiments of Renown to be led by Mancrusher Gargants to better accommodate 2000 point lists without dipping into Auxiliary options.

In the world of Kill Team, the highlights of the update were the changes made to TOmb World and additional errata for the Exodite Dragon Masters. For the Exodites, the new errata and rules commentary finally clears up some of the biggest lingering rules questions for the team, most importantly by making it clear just how exactly gaining cover works. As for Tomb World, multiple teams were updated so that breaching was brought in line with operate hatch for purposes of action restrictions or triggering ploys, and the pillars for Tomb World were updated to now count as cover, which opens up some very interesting new cover possibilities on Tomb World and could be a problem for shooting teams.

For more of our thoughts on the Kill Team update, check out our hot take on the changes!

Credit: BuffaloChicken

Mike Stewart Wins Telford Grand Tournament with Sylvaneth in Quiet Weekend for Events

Things were relatively quiet over the weekend for both the Age of Sigmar and Kill Team tournament scenes globally. But just because it was quiet doesn’t mean there’s nothing to cover.

While not as expansive as one of Games Workshop's marquee Open events, the new National Tournament series in the UK drew some big competition this weekend in Telford. 24 players in total battled out over five rounds, with Mike Stewart taking home the gold with an undefeated Sylvaneth list that leaned on the big heroes of the faction, including Alarielle, Drycha, and Belthanos. Mike’s win here continues a trend of very strong Sylvaneth performances in the current metagame, particularly with the big tree heroes list archetype like the one run by Mike.

As for some of the other large tournaments this weekend we have two singles events with over thirty players to look at, one in Oslo and one in Mexico. While both featured at least one Sylvaneth 4-1 player, the tree elves didn’t take home the gold at either event, with Kuba Kostrubiec’s Lumineth taking top prize at 2D6 Carnage in Oslo and Matt Nguyen winning Warhammex GT 2026 with his Slaves to Darkness. Congratulations to Mike, Matt, and Kuba for taking home the gold at their respective events!

Warmachine: Protectorate of Menoth Covenant of the Flame - Scourge of the Unbeliever

The Protectorate of Menoth Return to Warmachine

One of the most notable absences from Warmachine MK IV, the crusading zealots of the Protectorate of Menoth, finally made their triumphant return to the game last week with the release of the defenders of the flame box set, alongside standalone releases for the Revenger Light Warjack and the Crusader Heavy Warjack.

The new Protectorate of Menoth faction, the Covenant of the Flame, is led by the ambitious firebrand Feora and her closest cronies, and on the table the play much like the Protectorate of old with new twists. Like their original incarnation, Covenant of the Flame loves controlling the battlefield and setting things on fire, with the Four Gifts of Menoth army rule handing out one of four denial abilities each turn within your leaders control range to force your opponent to adjust their plans, and each leader having a unique way their army can consume fire tokens to boost their own performance and potential.

For more on the return of the Protectorate and how they were designed for the current incarnation of Warmachine, we sat down with Warmachine’s lead designer Jamie Perkins for an interview where he provided some very interesting thoughts on game design, Warmachine's appeal, and his own history with the Protectorate.

The Girls Are Fighting (You) at the MCP Fall Into the Multiverse GT

Halloween has always been one of the biggest weekends of the year for super heroes. After all, when else will you see so many Spider-Men running around the streets, on the prowl for candy?

Well this year it looks like Crisis Protocol is loathe to get left out of the fun, and hosted one of the bigger events of the weekend over at Element Games in Manchester, the Fall Into the Multiverse Official GT. This 6 round event hosted 37 players over the course of the weekend, with all corners of the Marvel universe showing up to fight for the grand prize, befitting an event named Fall Into the Multiverse.

Once the dust settled, Jim Gradwell took the top spot with his undefeated Avengers Affiliation crew that featured exclusively some of the most dangerous women in Marvel. Jim’s list, which he named “Smashing 4th walls and sometimes Matt Murdoch,” leaned exclusively on the ladies of the Avengers to draw from for his games, including She-Hulk, Captain Marvel, Wasp, Valkyrie, and Nebula, to bring home the top prize at the weekend event. Congratulations to Jim for the win!

title: Magic: The Gathering is hesitant to make Modern Horizons 4
content:
Magic: The Gathering's head designer has (more-or-less) confirmed that a new Modern Horizons set isn't currently in the works, writing on his blog that a Modern Horizons 4 set is an If, not a When.

These direct-to-modern sets have in the past been immensely popular, but also extremely controversial, and for much the same reason: they are full of powerful, format-warping cards.

While it's since been outpaced by sets like Final Fantasy and Lord of the Rings, back in 2022, Rosewater revealed that Modern Horizons 2 was the best-selling set of all time. Turns out power creep sells. As Magic has seen huge growth during this new UB era, it's likely that some of the best-performing in-universe premier sets like Tarkir Dragonstorm have now topped it too.

While they were great for Wizards' bottom line, Modern Horizons sets sparked a great deal of complaining from Modern players online. These fans were used to seeing relevant Modern cards trickle into their format gradually, as each Standard release provided perhaps one or two newcomers worth testing out.

Throwing a full 300-card release of highly relevant cards into this system was like plonking a dragon into a delicate British woodland of hedgehogs and squirrels. It upset the whole ecosystem and risked burning everything down.

For many fans, these releases removed a major reason to play a non-rotating format: that your deck, once invested in, would remain powerful and relevant for years to come.

The number of cards from Modern Horizons sets that now litter the MTG banlist is a testament to the idea that WotC may have pushed things a bit too far, and it sounds like now they're hesitant to go in this direction again. This is not the first time Rosewater has expressed this view, either. In August 2025, he mentioned off-hand that Wizards was "moving away" from direct-to-Modern sets.

On the other hand, the change in strategy may have nothing to do with the impact Modern Horizons 1, 2, or 3 had on the Modern format. It could just be that Wizards is less interested in creating cards for Constructed formats that aren't Standard. It has bigger money-makers to concern itself with these days.

Currently, it seems like Standard-legal Universes Beyond sets have more or less filled the space that might previously have been used for supplemental products like Modern Horizons - with Horizons and Remastered sets both going the way of the dodo.

Would you relish a Modern Horizons 4 or does the thought fill you with dread? Let us know over on the Wargamer Discord.

title: Tabletop Battles Reviews: Mycopunk
content:
When’s the last time you were killed by a microwave? For me, it was two hours ago after massacring my way through a horde of other betentacled appliances. Unfortunately, the humble microwave had been spared my full wrath and grafted the limb of a fallen comrade, which was driven into my back in vengeance.

Mycopunk is what happens when Borderlands and Deep Rock Galactic love each other very much. It is a co-op looter shooter where you take on the lethal fungi of a planet for the good of a company that is probably morally fine. Don't worry about it. You play as one of five characters with their own unique abilities. They all have some sort of movement tech and can all use the same weapons. By default, they’re quite basic because the real meat of the game is in the moment-to-moment gameplay and the upgrade system.

I Like the Way You Move

Let’s start with the gameplay. As a general rule of thumb, I value the feel of a game highly, especially movement and traversal. If controlling your character isn’t fun, the rest of the game is going to suffer as a result. Thankfully, moving around in Mycopunk is fun as hell. Deep Rock Galactic – a game very clearly in the DNA of Mycopunk – is all about claustrophobic corridors and relentless, grinding onslaughts; Mycopunk is the opposite. Missions are on wide open maps and you can absolutely haul ass through them. Even things like grinding on pipelines is noticeably faster than in comparable games.

And then there’s the vehicles. The initial vehicle, a hoverbike called the Blitseg, is like the Mass Effect Mako on meth. You don’t crash with the Blitseg, but it will always try to reorient itself to face the closest ground or ground-shaped object, so hitting a wall makes you spin wildly as you briefly go horizontal and maintain speed. Like the Mako, it requires you to be pure of heart to pilot it (there’s a definite learning curve) but once you're familiar with how it behaves, you'll have a blast going full-out and looping around jutting plateaus and boulders. To be honest, I didn’t try the other vehicles because I was having so much fun with my psychotic hoverbike.

Speaking of things that feel good, the gunplay is very satisfying. You have your basic revolver, your basic shotgun, your basic burst-fire assault rifle, your basic chainsaw, your basic plate-firing railgun… hang on.

This game accomplishes something that is genuinely hard to do; making a sci-fi arsenal that both feels high tech and is also unique. The weapons are inventive and each has its own flair. Even the generic assault rifle has a sort of spiral pattern to its bullets that makes it feel unique. And that’s all before you get into the almost six hundred upgrades that are available for both you and your guns.

Upgrading Upgrades

It is hard to make an upgrade system that feels inventive. Mycopunk pulls it off. Each upgrade is its own pattern, which you can place into a grid for each weapon and character. It turns the generic upgrade system into its own block puzzle, where builds aren’t just about the best combinations, but what combinations fit. Pigeons at Play made the very smart design decision to pair generic stat buffs with interesting gameplay changes.

Take the Glider, my personal favorite character. You can unlock the ability to move substantially fast if you glide backwards, boosting your ability to kite. In addition, that same unlock gives you a percentile increase to a stat like health or run speed. You can tech to make yourself an incredible medic who gets massive boosts to speed and strength while carrying downed players, with missiles that heal other players when they hit. Or you can have your missiles ricochet between enemies and even turn into bombs while flying.

All this frenetic gameplay does lead me to my one major complaint/word of advice. The default settings for the game turn it into a motion sickness simulator. I have legitimately never gotten motion sick from a game before, but the combination of the extremely narrow default FoV, the fisheye lens effect, and the innate head bobbing made me almost immediately nauseous. Thankfully, you can adjust these settings (though the fisheye does stay regardless; a stylistic choice that I can’t say I’m a fan of, but it certainly does make you feel more immersed in the world).

I also think the missions can become stale. The combat and progression systems keeps the game fresh, but after the tenth satellite salvage mission it felt more chore-like than I was hoping. I would have loved more story missions or a stronger guiding hand in the beginning. After the introductory mission I returned to the hub and was confused as to what I was supposed to do next because it just threw me into the full game.

Putting the Fun in Fungus

Now let’s talk about the thing that makes Mycopunk shine: the titular mycelium. The enemies in this game initially appear as generic appliances, but in reality, are the soft yellow center inside the machines. They each have random numbers and types of offensive and defensive protrusions, which you need to remove from them in order to reach that armored center. For basic enemies, you can usually just shoot them in the ‘face’, usually the screen or glass of the appliance. Alternatively, you can put enough firepower into a piece of them to blow it away and expose the center, which dies quickly once targeted.

The coolest part of all of this is the way other enemies will attach severed limbs to themselves to continue fighting. Dead Space, eat your heart out. The cartoonish art style does a lot to offset the legitimate horror of these enemies. Blow off three of the rusty metal limbs of one enemy, and it will slowly crawl towards you with the one remaining talon. All they want to do is kill. Sever the missile launching tendril of a boss and ignore it at your own peril, as one of the other weaker units will fuse with it and turn into a threat of its own. The system is genius and means combat stays fresh. Even if there are some base template enemies, anything can happen in the heat of battle and new threats can emerge. It really nails the feeling of a sentient hivemind. The individual pieces don’t matter; it will just keep growing and adapting unless you snuff out the source.

Substantive Style

The cell-shaded style and unique enemies and environments gives the game a look I’d consider ‘Charmingly Dirty’. The world is rusted, grimy, and poorly maintained; but at the same time the vibrant colors and cartoonish style makes it feel fun instead of grim. I think there is a version of this game that tries to lean into the horror aspects that are under the surface and makes the world dark both in delivery and lighting. That game would be worse than the one we have.

Indeed, every decision was made to focus on the charm of the game. Your handler, Roachard, is – as his name suggests – a cockroach, and the massive hub you spend your downtime in is filled with little jokes and world building. There’s even a projector that plays videos of other roaches engaged in everyday activities (it’s people dressed in fake roach costumes. It’s very funny).

Alongside that, the hub itself is ripe for exploration. I’m not joking about the size of the place; it took me probably a half hour to fully explore all the various rooms and minigames within.

Sometimes I’ll see games say they’re co-op between one to four players, and I’ll ask them if they mean their game is for groups-only or if you can play it solo. They’ll chuckle and say it’s a good co-op game, and then I’ll play it and see it was very clearly designed for groups. Mycopunk doesn’t have this problem. I spent a majority of my time in the game solo, and while I’m sure it would have been more fun with friends, that also describes everything that’s ever been made. Yeah, I’m playing with friends, of course it’s more fun. But the game absolutely works solo if that’s your prerogative.

Final Thoughts

Whether you’re looking for a new game for your friend-group, or just a well-made shooter to play on your own, Mycopunk delivers. While there are stronger single-player experiences out there that offer more crafted experiences, Mycopunk can absolutely go toe-to-toe with the juggernauts in the co-op looter shooter genre.
